utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Registrar, have the accused brought in, please. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: While the photographers are completing their work, I would like to know whether, first of all, the interpreters are relaxed and rested and ready to start this short week. Thank you. Does everybody hear me? Office of the Prosecutor, does the Defence hear? General Blaskic, do you hear?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLASKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume our work. I believe that Mr. Kehoe is going to do it today. The photographers have now gone out. All right Mr. Kehoe, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. President, your Honours. The first witness that the Office of the Prosecutor will call this morning is Mr. Payam Akhavan, A-K-H-A-V-A-N. Mr. Akhavan is now working for the Office of the Prosecutor and in fact, Mr. President, he has even appeared on several of the motions concerning some of the legal issues that we discussed at the outset of this case. Prior to that time, Mr. Akhavan had been involved in various humanitarian organisations acting as a humanitarian lawyer. He has an advanced degree on that subject. He was working in 1993 for the Commission on Human Rights, which was a commission that was part of the United Nations, that was called upon to examine human rights violations throughout the former Yugoslavia and then present those conclusions in writing to the United Nations and naturally to the international community at large. Mr. Akhavan, along with another individual by the name of Thomas Osorio, was called upon to travel to Central Bosnia in the first week of May 1993. In fact they arrived on 30th May 1993, to do an investigation concerning the events surrounding the massacre in Ahmici. They talked to a variety of individuals, they visited the location on various times, they spoke to the defendant, General Blaskic, they spoke to Mario Cerkez, the brigade commander of the Viteska Brigade and they likewise spoke to Dario Kordic, who is the Vice-President of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the HVO. All three individuals denied responsibility or that the HVO could have been involved, among other things. The conclusions of this field team were sent back to Geneva, where a report concerning the events in Ahmici, as well as a report concerning events of an alleged Muslim killing in the village of Miletici were presented and it was ultimately reduced to a report and published on 19th May 1993 by the Commission on Human Rights. That is essentially the testimony of Mr. Akhavan we will be presenting today. We have a copy of that report that was published by the Commission on Human Rights in, of course, both French and English that we would present to the court as an exhibit. That is the substance of Mr. Akhavan's testimony. On an administrative note, Mr. President, over the weekend we discovered a -- there was a statement. We discovered that one of the statements, an interview had not been turned over to the Defence. The reason it had not been turned over to the Defence was that it had never been signed or read by Mr. Akhavan until Saturday and we took it upon ourselves to get it to the Defence. The statement that had been turned over to the Defence was a statement that was signed by Mr. Akhavan and that was the one that had been processed by the ICTY and that was the one that was retrieved from the computer. In any event, the Prosecutor did give this to the Defence, I called him yesterday and provided it to the Defence. I bring that to the court's attention so it might resolve any problems in that regard before we bring Mr. Akhavan in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, do you wish to make a comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do, your Honour. We do not wish to delay the examination, we wish to go ahead and we simply note for the record that the statement, regardless of whether it was adopted, was subject to the court's disclosure order of 27th January of this year, which stated that regardless of the form of a statement, whether it has been adopted, signed, whatever, it must be produced. So it does not matter if the witness had not read it. So long as it was not a work of fiction by the investigator but in fact was based on an interview with the witness, it should have been produced. It also contains statements of the accused which are new and different from the other statement of this witness which was produced. I will file a copy of this statement under seal, I think it needs to be in the record that this was not produced in a timely manner, but we do not wish to delay the proceedings, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let us not put in motion after motion. You know we have already received many of them. Try to settle things right away. Let us not make an incident out of everything, please. The judges are here in order to seek responsibility, to see whether General Blaskic is responsible in this adversarial system here with both parties here. First of all I would like to know whether you had the essential part of the statements. How many statements did Mr. Akhavan make? What did you give to the Defence and what did you not? Was it important, was it given today, can you have him brought back? Anyway, he is here, he can be brought back if necessary. Mr. Kehoe, could you explain the matters so we can settle this incident immediately. Mr. Kehoe, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The first statement that was actually written by Mr. Akhavan, dated 13th December 1994, was handed over to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Okay, 13th December 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The other statement was a statement taken after an interview on 23rd June 1995 that Mr. Akhavan had not read until this past Saturday, and this past Saturday, I am talking about 13th December 1997, nor has he ever signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Here I have to say that the Defence would find this a bit strange. He is in the Office of the Prosecutor, the second one was read by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Do you hear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It was in your favour, it is too bad you did not hear it. I will repeat myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will read it, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, the second statement of 23rd June 1995, which was read by him on Saturday, we do have to say that this is a bit annoying, we have to admit that. Let us try to work in such a way that there is kind of fluidity in the discussions otherwise incidents arise. It was disclosed today, is that right, Mr. Kehoe? This statement was disclosed today?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It was disclosed yesterday. I believe I called Mr. Hayman yesterday afternoon and he said he would pick it up around 6.00. That is what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Explain to us, is it fundamentally different from the one of December 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is not fundamentally different. There are additional details concerning the conversations with the accused, yes, there are. I raise this point, Mr. President, if counsel feels prejudiced in any fashion, we can certainly delay the testimony of Mr. Akhavan until counsel is prepared to move forward. Mr. Akhavan is working in the Office of the Prosecutor, we had notified Defence counsel that he would be a witness this week. Nevertheless, to assure that there is absolutely no prejudice to the Defence, we will delay the witness's testimony until the Defence counsel, Mr. Hayman, is prepared to move forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I will consult my colleagues for a moment. (Pause). All right, I have the agreement of my colleagues that we will settle this right now without having to have a motion. The second statement means that the Defence has to see whether it is very different from the other statement, in terms of the requirements of General Blaskic, that is to see whether it is very different. If it is very different, Mr. Hayman, you would be able to bring the witness back for your cross-examination. He only has to come down two flights of stairs, so it would not be very difficult. If you agree, Mr. Hayman, perhaps you could spare the Tribunal having to read yet another motion. We have now resolved this incident. We can now have the witness brought in. Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I do not intend to file a motion, your Honour, but I am going to file the two statements for the Appellate Chamber, should there ever be an appeal in this case, so they can see what material statements of the accused were not made available to the Defence. I am not filing a motion, but let the record be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let us not start thinking about appeals already, we have a lot to do with the first trial. Of course, you will appeal if you want to, but let us wait. All this seems to me to be much ado about nothing. Let us try to settle as many incidents as possible here among ourselves and avoid written documents. In any case, what you have said has been put into the transcript, do not fear. Mr. Kehoe, let us now have the witness brought in. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please tell us your name and first name again. We do know it, of course, but it is for the record. You did not hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would certainly hope so. You are in the Office of the Prosecutor and it has two official languages, French and English. Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Please give us your name and your first name for the transcript, so these things are done according to form. You are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My surname is Akhavan, my first name is Payam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, please read the solemn statement that the usher is going to give you that is your oath. MR. PAYAM AKHAVAN (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Akhavan, please be seated. In accordance with new proceedings for statements that are now in effect in this Trial Chamber -- do you hear me? The Prosecutor has given us the general content of your statement. During your statement, do not omit, as far as form goes, the fact that there was a second statement which apparently you only read last Saturday, which is something that the Tribunal has just learned and which it regrets. As regards the second statement of 23rd June 1995, please during your statement do not lose sight of the fact that there is a second statement which was disclosed only yesterday afternoon to the Defence, apparently. Please do not lose sight of that. Mr. Kehoe has explained the general content of your testimony inter alia the framework of your mission during which, on behalf of the Commission of Human Rights in May 1993, you were able to investigate into massacres, or at least violations of international criminal law in Ahmici, and in addition, another part of your statement, please speak about the different conversations you had with various officials, including the accused. You wrote a report to Geneva. This was given to the Defence, Mr. Kehoe, was it not, that report? That is the report of 19th May 1993 to the Commission on Human Rights. It was a public report, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a public report, Mr. President, and it is published by the individuals in Geneva, mainly based on the information provided by Mr. Akhavan. But this is not Mr. Akhavan's report, it is the report of the Commission for Human Rights, the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: For the record, it was not given to us and I do not believe it is specifically identified in his statement. I think we found it from public records, but we will see if in fact we were able to find it, based on the information provided in the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: These are part of the public documents that are indicated by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and which do not always give rise to the need for mutual disclosure. We have noted this. Mr. Kehoe, perhaps you have some prior questions you would like to ask and after that, the witness will make his statement in one -- in a single statement, without interrupting him, unless you feel it absolutely necessary. Is the Defence ready? All right, you may proceed, Mr. Kehoe. Examined by MR. KEHOE

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. Akhavan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, at this point you work for the Office of the Prosecutor, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have a background in humanitarian law, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact you have worked on various legal issues involved in the Blaskic case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, prior to coming to the Office of the Prosecutor, can you give the judges an idea of your involvement in humanitarian law as it pertains to human rights issues, both on a legal and a practical level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prior to the joining the Office of the Prosecutor, I had spent several years doing work in the field of human rights and humanitarian law. That included academic and practical work. The academic work involved post graduate legal studies in the field of international human rights law. It also involved being research associate at the Norwegian and Danish Human Rights Institute. I also during this period participated in a number of human rights fact-finding missions, including one in the region of Nagorno Karabach, which was in what was then the Soviet Union and prior to joining the UN Centre for Human Rights in April 1993, I had been on two missions for the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe, CSCE, which is presently known as the OSCE, Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe. One of these missions was under the leadership of Hans Kurel and it involved looking at violations of humanitarian law in the former Yugoslavia. The second mission was under the leadership of the then Ambassador, Tadeusz Mazowiecki, in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On a practical level, Mr. Akhavan, if we could have a delay between my question and your answer, because we just have to wait until the interpreters catch up. So if there is a delay between the questioning, that is what I am waiting for. So it would be fair to say prior to your work with the Commission on Human Rights, you had experience working on various human rights issues in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was for that purpose that I was recruited by the Centre for Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Talk to us, if you will, about when you began to work with the Commission on Human Rights; what is the Commission on Human Rights, what is the mandate for that Commission and what methodology is employed by the Commission when it writes its report and attempts to come to certain conclusions. Would you do that for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Human Rights Commission is a sessional body of the United Nations, operating under the Economic and Social Council of the United Nations. It is a body of member states approximately 53, who meet once every year between February and March in order to discuss human rights issues globally. There are two sorts of mandates which the Human Rights Commission confers upon so-called special rapporteurs who are appointed by the Commission to prepare expert reports on various themes. There are so-called thematic mandates which look at a certain theme, such as extra judicial killings, torture and so on and so forth, and then there are who are country rapporteurs, who are assigned a particular country to investigate. In this particular case, after the war broke out in the former Yugoslavia, in the summer of 1992, there was an extraordinary session of the Commission held, during which time the commission established what was perhaps the broadest mandate to investigate allegations of humanitarian law violations in the former Yugoslavia. To this end, they appointed the former Polish Prime Minister, Tadeusz Mazowiecki, as this special rapporteur, and put at his disposal the broadest possible resources for discharging his mandate. The mandate of a special rapporteur is not to look at individual criminal liability, but to look at so-called state responsibility, to try and provide accurate information as to whether states are discharging their obligations under international law in terms of complying with international human rights standards. In the case of armed conflict, where the state becomes fractured, as was the case in Bosnia-Herzegovina, where the so-called legitimate government may actually control a very small portion of the territory, state responsibility can also be attributed to authorities which are in de facto control of a particular area, even if they are not internationally recognised states. The methodology in general is to look at the broadest possible sources of information in order to gather reliably attested evidence of human rights violations. The special rapporteur has a quasi judicial function. He or she must act both as, if you like, Prosecution, Defence and judge in arriving at his or her conclusions. The special rapporteur, in the case of the former Yugoslavia, because of the large volume of information, would have to operate through a large number of staff. In this case there were approximately five or six staff members when I joined the mandate. At this point in time, there may be as many as 20 people. The staff or the special rapporteur directly receives information from various sources and then decides what weight to attribute to these, based on the reliability of the source, based on whether other sources have corroborated the evidence given elsewhere. The sources generally include, in a situation such as that of the former Yugoslavia, the international observers such as UNPROFOR who may be on the ground, who are neutral in the sense that they do not have a particular interest in the outcome of the conflict. They involve, other than UNPROFOR, the staff of international humanitarian organisations, such as the UN High Commissioner for Refugees. They could involve other intergovernmental organisations such as the European Community Monitoring Mission. In certain cases, they can involve non-governmental organisations conducting investigations in the field. This would include Amnesty International, it would include Human Rights Watch. Of course, information is also received from governmental sources, but generally information which is received from governments or parties to the conflict are treated with extreme caution, and, of course, the most important source of information are direct victims and witnesses as survivors who may give eyewitness accounts of what has transpired in the region. If I may just add one other element to the methodology, when we are dealing with state responsibility or the responsibility of a party to the conflict, it is not altogether irrelevant to look at the role which particular individuals in positions of leadership may be playing. We will inevitably try to get evidence as to which party is in factual control of a given territory, and then to try and ascertain who are the individuals who are determining the policy, whether civilian or military, in that particular region. This allows us with greater certainty to determine which party may have been responsible for a particular atrocity or human rights violation; whether through having ordered such atrocity or through having acquiesced in such atrocity. But we would never in these reports actually name any individuals, because the purpose of the report is not to determine individual criminal liability, but to look at the responsibility of the parties to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Using the methodology that you just discussed, were you and another colleague of yours called upon to go to the Vitez area in late April and early May to look into the events concerning the crimes that took place in the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, approximately one week after my arrival in the former Yugoslavia in Zagreb, we were approached by members of the European Community Monitoring Mission, in addition to the fact that we had already seen media reports of what had happened in the Lasva Valley region, which had become particularly notorious because of one family which apparently had been burnt alive in the basement of their home. Because of the tremendous media attention being given to the events in the Lasva Valley region, we were encouraged to conduct an impartial investigation of the events in the region. My impression was that the ECMM because more interested in stabilising the situation, politically and militarily through having an impartial account of what had transpired, but, of course, our interest was more directly related to a human rights investigation which would provide an accurate report of what had transpired, irrespective of the consequences which that may have for stabilisation or normalisation of relations in that region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went to that area on 30th April 1993, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the judges what you did, where you went, who you spoke to and the results and conclusions that you arrived at, in your own words, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On April 30th, we flew by UNPROFOR air transport to Sarajevo from Zagreb, and we were taken to Kiseljak at the UNPROFOR base, where we were met by members of the British battalion. That same evening, on April 30th, after dinner, we were taken by the British battalion to Vitez, where the British battalion was based. The mode of transport was a series of Warrior tanks which the British battalion used through the region. I mention this to explain that in the very first evening when we arrived in Vitez, we could already see through the very small porthole which exists in the tank that a number of houses were on fire in the vicinity of Vitez. I imagine that it was Vitez, because it was just several minutes away from arriving at the base. I was told by some of the British soldiers that these were houses which apparently had been set on fire, and they were almost certainly the homes of Muslims and that these sort of activities had been taking place in the region for the past several days. During the stay, before I explain to your Honours the particular meetings which we had, the particular locations which we visited, our methodology was largely to try and speak as often as possible with members of the British battalion. We would spend a lot of time during lunch, during dinner in informal discussions with soldiers as well as commanders to get a better idea of what the overall situation was in the Lasva Valley region. We spoke with the higher ranking commanders very often in order to get the overall perspective of the situation in the region, and in particular, to get an idea of whether there was a great deal of lawlessness and chaos which could possibly explain some of the violations, or whether the military commanders were in firm control of the region. We spoke very often to the lower ranking soldiers in order to get a better appreciation of the situation on the ground, and very often, the soldiers would give us a much more accurate account of what the situation was from the daily trips which they would make in the region, and after six months, they had gained great familiarity with the actors and the general situation in the Lasva Valley. I should point out that at this time when we were arriving, the Cheshire Regiment was about to be rotated and a new regiment was beginning to arrive, the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment. Very often they would have joint patrols so that the Cheshire Regiment could share with the incoming Prince of Wales' Own Regiment their expert knowledge about the region. The first day on May 1st, we were taken on a joint patrol between the Cheshire and Prince of Wales regiment, to look at the region of Vitez and some of the neighbouring villages. I believe that during this first tour, we were accompanied by, I believe it was Sergeant Watters, I may have the military ranking -- I may not have correctly said his military ranking, but he was the second in command from Colonel Stewart. I believe that Alistair Duncan, who was the commander of the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment was also accompanying us in the tank. We toured the region for a few hours. Because of the ever present danger of sniper fire, it was not always possible for us to stick our head out of the tank, if you like, and to have a free look at what existed in the surrounding area, but on occasion, the members of the tank crew would indicate to us a sight which would be of particular interest. We drove by, that day, the village of Ahmici, and it was unmistakable because of the minaret, which had been destroyed in the village, minaret which had been literally broken at the base and which had been leaning over another building in the village. When we drove by Ahmici, we noticed that there were a number of men in military uniform, and they appeared to be looting, going from house to house taking out whatever property of value they could find. We were told by the members of the British battalion that those were almost certainly members of the HVO, the Bosnian Croat armed forces. We spent the evening further speaking with members of the British battalion, and the base in Vitez was such that a number of other staff of a number of other international agencies would congregate there during meal times, so we could speak there with members of the ECMM, of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, sometimes non-governmental organisations which were conducting their own fact-finding investigations and very often members of the media who had great familiarity with the region. We tried to get as much information as we could that evening in anticipation of a more detailed on site investigation of Ahmici on the following day, that being May 2nd. On May 2nd, we were taken to the village of Ahmici, with two Scimitars, which were armoured personnel carriers. I should mention that the reason why we looked at Ahmici in particular is because we had obviously very limited resources. We were only two staff members, myself and my colleague Thomas Osorio, which were responsible for investigating all violations in the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. By necessity, we had to prioritise our investigations, especially in a war which involved such widespread atrocities. We were aware, prior to going to the Lasva Valley region, that there were allegations on both sides that atrocities had been committed against civilians. There were allegations by the Croats that the members of the Bosnian army had committed atrocities against their civilians, including the alleged incarceration of several hundred civilians in Zenica, which was under the control of the Bosnian government. We chose to prioritise the events in Vitez and Ahmici because according to the information which we had received, that was where the largest number of killings had taken place. There were actually no allegations on the part of the Croats that, for example, in Zenica any significant number of people had been killed. The only allegations were that of forced expulsions of Croats from their homes and their detention in certain holding centres, but in the case of Ahmici and Vitez, we had received reliable accounts which suggested that several hundred civilians may have been massacred, so that was the reason for prioritising that village. When we went to Ahmici, we noticed that of the approximately 200 homes, that only 15 to 20 were undamaged. Practically every other building had been destroyed, in many cases -- I would say in almost every case it had been set on fire and the roof had collapsed and we noticed, of course, immediately that both of the mosques in the village had also been destroyed, one of them by means of an explosion, the minaret as I explained, and the other a church in the upper part of the village had apparently also been gutted by fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A church or a mosque?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, a mosque. There were two mosques, one with a minaret, one without. The mosque in the lower part of the village was the one with the minaret and the mosque in the upper part of the village was the one which apparently had been gutted by fire. We noticed that there were numerous animals which had been killed, a lot of livestock which was rotting in buildings in the middle of the road. We noticed that many of the homes still had their clothes' line with their laundry hanging in the wind, which suggested that the people had left in an awful hurry, there was no time really for the people to prepare for what had awaited them. We obviously smelled the stench of rotting bodies; there were still apparently numerous bodies which had not been recovered from the buildings, and there was, as people would say, a smell of death in the village. We noticed that some of the buildings were still smouldering, even two weeks after the attack, and we were under the impression that many of the buildings had been set on fire with flammable liquid, such as petroleum, because of the deep shiny black colour of the wood which remained in the buildings. Maybe I should mention that one of the first places we investigated in the village was on the main road in the southern part of the village, the main road which goes from Vitez to -- I am not sure if it is -- it goes to Kiseljak. I am not sure of the intermediate destination, whether it is Busovaca or Dubravica, but that was the main road you had to take in order to get to the village. We were told by the members of the British battalion, those present with us as well as those who we had spoken to earlier, that between this road and the Catholic cemetery, which was on the southern part of the road, was an open field where they had discovered at least 20 bodies and this was the field where they had discovered the body of one mother holding her child and practically speaking all the bodies they had recovered were those of elderly people or women and children. From the account which we had from the British battalion and from the on site investigation, we began to construct a story of how the attack had transpired. We noticed that there was a great deal of damage from what appeared to be mortar shelling in the northern part of the village. The northern part of the village led to some hills and some forests where people could escape to and hide, and it appeared as if the mortar shelling had forced the inhabitants to either remain in their home or to escape towards a southerly direction towards the main road, since the artillery bombardment was in the northern part of the village. It appeared that a number of those people who had been found by the British battalion in that field which I had mentioned across from the Catholic cemetery had been ambushed, that the snipers were lying in wait for them to come out, so that they would be killed. We noticed that in a depression in a hollow beside the field there was an ideal position where snipers could have an excellent vantage point for killing these people, and surely we found what would be at least 100 to 200 spent casings of bullets, which suggested that snipers had been positioned there. We subsequently went from house to house to assess the kind of damage which had been done, and we noticed that on average, in front of every home, there were, let us say, 50 spent shell casings, suggesting that a large amount of ammunition had been used and suggesting that the ammunition had been used at the doorstep literally of the homes, and it was not away from the residential areas that the ammunition was used. We noticed also that there were spent shells from rocket-propelled grenades, which are unmistakable because of their very large size. In certain cases, we also noticed shell casings from anti-aircraft guns, which were frequently used in the former Yugoslavia against civilians, civilian targets, against personnel rather than against aircraft. At a certain point, we noticed that one elderly woman with two young boys, which could have been her grandchildren, was walking through a path in the village. My colleague Thomas, who spoke Serbo-Croatian, decided to approach this lady to try and see if she was willing to speak to us, whether she knew something about what had happened in Ahmici on April 16th, whether she knew some of the perpetrators. When we approached her, a few seconds later we heard sniper fire, which apparently was directed towards us and at that point we realised that someone did not want us in the village investigating the atrocities, and we began to run away and under heavy sniper fire managed to make it back to the Scimitar and one of the soldiers that was with us was struck by a bullet, fortunately only grazed, and I believe there was even a camera crew to record this whole episode. At that point, we were unable to find the source of sniper fire and returned back to the British battalion base, having gained a very good impression of the sort of attack which had taken place in Ahmici. Having looked, if you like, at the physical evidence, we decided the following day to try and locate some of the survivors. On May 3rd, we went with the British battalion across the front-line to Zenica, which was under Bosnian government control. We went to, I believe, the institute for war crimes, I forget the exact name, but it was an institute which was established in order to document war crimes in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and through them, we managed to locate about 100 of the survivors from Ahmici, who were now at a refugee collection centre in Zenica. These 100 people were predominantly elderly, women and children. I do not recall having seen any men in their midst. They had been detained in a school in Dubravica, I believe, for about two weeks prior to being released, and they had just arrived a few days earlier from their detention. They had indicated that during their detention, that there was not necessarily serious mistreatment amounting to torture or anything of that nature, but that they were not really adequately fed and some of them indicated to us that at least two women in their midst had been taken away and apparently raped by members of the HVO. We spoke with these people for several hours to get an eyewitness account of what had happened, and then to try to juxtapose that account with the physical evidence which we had seen in Ahmici. Practically all of the people indicated to us that at about 5.30 am in the morning, around the time when the morning prayers were being said from the minaret in the village, that they had heard explosions, and that many of them had escaped from their homes. Some had seen those who had been killed in the field which I described, and others said that the only reason they survived is because they managed to escape somewhere into the forest and to hide, so that the HVO soldiers did not find them. They said that after the bombardment, the soldiers went door to door, in certain cases they would throw grenades into homes or set the homes on fire and when the occupants would come out of the homes, they would simply execute them right there. One of them suggested that a soldier who told her father to come out of the house on the promise that he would not be harmed and when he opened the door, he was immediately shot. I think that there was only one case where the people were not killed in an act of apparent mercy by one of the soldiers who knew the wife of the man he had just killed and the children and who spared their lives and simply told them to run away, but in practically every other case, it appeared that where the soldiers could kill an individual, that they would, not spare any lives. We had one testimony which was particularly useful. That was the testimony of an elderly man who apparently had sustained burns on his hands and feet and the side of his body. His name was Sakib Ahmic. He was one of the people in the collection centre in Zenica. He explained that during the attack, he had hidden behind a sofa in the home of, I forget whether it was his son or daughter, anyway in the home of his child, and that he could clearly see the soldiers come through the house, go into the adjoining room and he heard bullets and then saw the man and woman fall on the ground, though he was not certain whether they had died or not, he clearly saw they were shot by the soldiers. There were also two children in that home aged, I believe, four or six months and the other about three to four years of age and he was not sure what had become of them, whether they also had been killed or not. In any event, he said that the house was subsequently set on fire through the use of some sort of flammable liquid, petroleum perhaps, and that he managed somehow to escape after the house had been set on fire and to hide in a hollow in the village before making it to Zenica. I should mention that subsequently on May 5th, my colleague came back and further interviewed Sakib Ahmic and another lady, who I believe bore some relation to him, and got exact details as to the location of the home in the village and as to the location of the bodies within that home, which allowed us finally on May 6th, in a subsequent visit to Ahmici, to locate the body of the man, woman and the infant and the child, which further gave credence to the accuracy and veracity of the testimony of the survivors. Subsequent to May 3rd -- I beg your pardon, I should also mention that practically speaking, every survivor that we spoke with testified that the soldiers who were involved in the killings were wearing army uniforms and that all of them were members of the HVO in the sense that they had the familiar armband of the circle with the red and white chequered flag with the HVO sign. Almost all of them said that they could see that these were HVO soldiers and just to be 100 per cent sure, we even asked them whether they could identify by name some of the perpetrators to discount the possibility that these people could have been from some other paramilitary group, simply donning HVO uniforms, and we managed to get, in the limited time available, the names of 18 perpetrators given to us, and many of these perpetrators were from Ahmici itself, or from the surrounding villages, which proved to us conclusively that what had transpired in Ahmici had been a deliberate, concerted large-scale military attack which had required, according to the military experts which we spoke with, probably a company of 100 to 150 soldiers, the use of artillery, the use of several thousand rounds of ammunition, and that the perpetrators were indeed members of the HVO. On May 4th, in order to ensure that we had not simply looked at one-sided sources of evidence, we asked the British battalion to take us to some of the isolated Croatian villages and hamlets to try and do an investigation of human rights violations committed against Croats. We discovered in the hamlet of Miletici, which was a very small community in the vicinity of Vitez, that a group of so-called Mujahedin, which were apparently recruited from the local population but also they were foreign mercenaries, had attacked Miletici not so much by means of weaponry but had simply come into the village, had taken out three or four young Croatian men who were of fighting age, had tortured them and beheaded them. We went to the home where the beheading had taken place and we took note of the human rights violations in our report. So by May 4th, I think we had a good overall perspective of what had happened in the Lasva Valley region, and a sense of the atrocities which had been committed by the HVO against the local Muslim population and what appeared to be isolated acts of revenge or retaliation by small numbers of Muslim forces and we were not able to ascertain whether the Muslim forces were agents of the Bosnian government, in the sense that they were regular members of the army, or whether they were simply isolated individuals operating on their own. It was very clear, though, that the attack on Miletici was a very small scale attack which could have been committed by a band of four or five people, which indeed was the case, whereas the attack on Ahmici was necessarily a large scale attack which required tremendous military preparation. I should also add that one of the problems in the region was that virtually speaking, every man of military age was wearing a uniform, either of the HVO or of the Bosnian army, and that it was very difficult in certain cases to distinguish who is a combatant and who is a non-combatant, in terms of people who may have died. You were not always able to tell whether they were a combatant in the sense that they were a member of an organised armed attack or resistance, or whether they were simply locals who were home for the weekend to visit their families and who simply happened to have their uniform on, but in any event, our impression was that where there was resistance to the HVO forces that it was very isolated resistance, that there was no large scale organised resistance within the villages, so they may not have been entirely undefended. But clearly they were defended to a very limited extent, by maybe the father of the home who will pick up a shotgun and try to defend his family against the oncoming army. I should also mention that we investigated also the situation in Vitez itself. We went to Stari Vitez, which was the, if you like, the Muslim part of the city which, of course, was heavily fortified at this point. After a number of attacks, including a truck bomb which had exploded some weeks earlier, which had caused extensive damage, as well as the events which transpired on April 16th. Stari Vitez was a heavily fortified part of the city where the Muslims were clearly in the defensive, ever ready to be attacked again by the HVO. We received evidence that in Vitez, up to that point, approximately 101 bodies had been identified and buried. According to the padre of the British battalion and other sources, of the 101 dead, 96 were Muslims and five were Croats. This I believe was very easy to corroborate, because the respective Muslim and Catholic priests had done the religious rituals for those who had died prior to their burial. In the case of Ahmici, we were told by the British battalion that they had uncovered approximately 89 bodies at that point in time, and, of course, because of the way in which the buildings had been destroyed, because of the existence of mines, possibly booby-traps, it was very difficult to dig underneath the rubble to discover many of the bodies and the British battalion simply did not have the resources to engage in massive investigation of where these bodies lay, but according to the account of the survivors in Zenica, there could have been up to 100 additional people who they themselves had seen executed, as opposed to people who were unaccounted for, that number being as high as 300, so it was conceivable, although we could never get accurate statistics, that up to 500 people, at least 200 and up to 500 people could have been killed in Ahmici. The population of Ahmici, as far as we could gather from 1991 census and other statistics available to us, was approximately 800, of whom the overwhelming majority, approximately 80 per cent, would have been Muslim and approximately 20 or possibly even 10 per cent would have been Croatian. In addition, there were approximately 300 displaced persons, almost exclusively Muslims, who had come from other regions of Bosnia-Herzegovina to stay with people in Ahmici, so the population was approximately 1,100, so it was very clear that a significant part of that community had been killed in this attack, anywhere from 20, 30 to 50 per cent of the population. This brings me to May 5th, which is perhaps one of the most important days in the investigation. On May 5th, my colleague Thomas and I decided to go separate ways in order to optimise on our limited time and resources. Thomas went back to further interview the survivors in Zenica, and he, as I explained earlier, managed to get further details of what had transpired on April 16th, including as I mentioned, the name of 18 alleged culprits, as well as specific information about the home in which we found the bodies of the family eventually on May 6th. At this point in time, I had requested the British battalion to arrange meetings with the Bosnian Croat or rather the HVO leadership in the region. They had told me that the three people which would be relevant in this area would be firstly Dario Kordic, who was the Vice-President of Herceg-Bosna and the HDZ political party; Colonel Blaskic, who at that time was the highest ranking military office in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone for the HVO, and Mario Cerkez, who was the head of the HVO in Vitez. The first meeting on May 5th was with Colonel Blaskic at his headquarters in Vitez. When I met with Colonel Blaskic, I believe that our meeting lasted approximately two hours during the morning. I noticed, of course, that there were a large number of HVO soldiers obviously at the headquarters. I noticed in the midst of these soldiers, as well the soldiers who were wearing black uniforms and according to my understanding -- as far as I knew at that point in time, these were members of the HOS paramilitary formation. I subsequently learned that they were known as the Vitezovi and they may not have gone under the name HOS, but they were still referred to commonly as HOS because of their counterparts in Croatia. My meeting with Colonel Blaskic consisted of two parts and maybe I can explain why I had insisted on meeting the HVO leadership. I had insisted on meeting them because I wanted to give them an opportunity, as was our practice in all human rights investigations, to counter the allegations which had been made against them, and to give us some possible alternative explanation as to what had happened, although at this stage of the investigation, everything led to the conclusion that there had been a concerted and planned HVO attack against civilians and civilian objects in the Lasva Valley region. So we wanted to give the leadership the opportunity to prove us wrong. I asked Colonel Blaskic about his formal status and his powers and his scope of responsibility. He explained to me that he was the commander of all HVO forces in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone and, of course, what we were primarily concerned with was the Lasva Valley region and indeed he confirmed that he was the commander of all HVO forces in the Lasva Valley region. I asked Colonel Blaskic about the existence of paramilitary formations. I wanted to make sure that there was no possibility that rogue elements who were not part of the HVO command may have committed the atrocities. He suggested to me that although there may have been some paramilitary formations that he was clearly in command of the Lasva Valley region and that no operation of any military significance could take place either without his consent or his knowledge. In short, I was told that he and his HVO subordinates were in clear control of the Lasva Valley region. At that point in time, I began to explain to Colonel Blaskic in great detail -- as I explained the meeting lasted approximately two hours -- I explained to him in great detail the evidence which we had uncovered in Ahmici and in Vitez with respect to atrocities against civilians. I explained to him -- I will not repeat, for the sake of brevity, here all of the details which I had earlier indicated concerning the way in which the attack had been carried out, how concerted and deliberate and well organised it was, what a large volume of ammunition had been used and so on and so forth and, of course, I emphasised the testimony of the approximately 50 to 60 survivors who we had spoken with in Zenica as to the identity of those perpetrators. Colonel Blaskic did not deny that atrocities had been committed in Ahmici. He did not try to persuade me that these atrocities had not occurred, but he adamantly denied that any of his soldiers would have been involved in such an operation. I repeated once again that all evidence linked HVO soldiers to that attack, and he repeated his position that as far as he was concerned, none of his soldiers would have committed such atrocities. This suggested not only that he, according to his own claim, had not ordered such an attack, but that his soldiers were really, if you like, well behaved soldiers who would not commit such atrocities. I asked Colonel Blaskic a number of other questions, and he confirmed to me, as we had been told by members of the British battalion and ECMM and other observers, that there really was no reason for any attack on Ahmici, in the sense that there was virtually no military presence whatsoever, there was no legitimate military target in Ahmici which would have justified an attack. At that point in time, somewhere between the halfway mark of the interview, a certain gentleman came into the room and I believe that that gentleman was Ante Valenta. I was told and I am not sure if my recollection is accurate, that he had been a school teacher prior to becoming involved actively with politics in the Lasva Valley region and that he may have published either a book or a booklet or a pamphlet which outlined, if you like, the ideology of the Bosnian Croat political establishment. Mr. Valenta interjected a few times. He, to the best of my memory, mentioned some things about how the Muslims had different values than the Croats, how in reality the Croatian were Europeans, they were civilised, whereas the Muslims were somehow less civilised, less European. It seemed to be some sort of apology, some sort of propaganda exercise which I , of course, ignored and I tried to direct my attention back to my discussion with Colonel Blaskic. At the end of the interview, I asked Colonel Blaskic who could have possibly committed the attacks on civilians in Ahmici as well as Vitez, and he was not really able to give me any alternative explanation, he simply told me that he did not know who did it and he was certain that his own soldiers did not. I explained to Colonel Blaskic in very clear terms that as commander of the HVO Armed Forces in the region, he was responsible to undertake an investigation, a full investigation to identify the perpetrators of these atrocities and that he was responsible as commander to ensure that these perpetrators were punished. My interest at that point was, of course, not to determine the individual criminal liability of anyone, that there was really no part of our mandate which made such an exercise relevant. Nor was there at that time an international criminal court or any other body for which we would have been interested in gathering evidence. My only concern at that point was to point out what is the responsibility of a state or, in the absence of a state, a para-state or substate entity such as Herceg-Bosna, but that responsibility under international law is to enforce human rights, not simply by constitutional means but to enforce human rights by punishing those who have violated human rights norms. So it was in that light that I reminded Colonel Blaskic of his responsibility to investigate and prosecute those who had been responsible. I met subsequently Mario Cerkez, who was the head of the HVO in Vitez. The meeting with him was somewhat shorter, but once again, I explained to him the detailed account of the evidence which we had uncovered and asked for an explanation. He did not offer me any explanation, but simply said that on April 16th, he had been sleeping when all of a sudden he heard gunfire and artillery fire and that when he woke up, there was chaos and he really did not know what was going on, everyone was killing everybody else, suggesting there really was no concerted military action and certainly nothing that he was aware of. Colonel Stewart subsequently joined this meeting and both Colonel Stewart and I also reminded Mario Cerkez that he is responsible with respect to those soldiers under his command to conduct a full investigation and to ensure that those who are responsible are brought to trial. The last meeting of that day was with Dario Kordic. It was a bit difficult to arrange a meeting with him and I had to wait outside of his office for almost one hour before a member of the British battalion persuaded him to have a meeting with me. The meeting with him was very short and abrupt, I would say 15 to 20 minutes. It was under very heavy guard. Mr. Kordic was wearing a military uniform, seated behind a desk with some of his soldiers. I explained very quickly to Mr. Kordic what our mandate was, explained to him once again the evidence of atrocities in the region and he suggested to me that the HVO soldiers could not conceivably have committed those crimes because, according to his own words, they were good Christians who would never commit such heinous atrocities. He then went on to suggest, when I asked him whether he had any explanations, that the atrocities were committed either by Serbs, who would have infiltrated the region at night in order to commit this atrocity, which I found very difficult to believe because it would have involved the movement of some 100 to 150 soldiers with mortar, with weaponry, undetected through really the nerve centre of HVO control, to have killed all of these people and then to have retreated without anyone having noticed them. He then suggested that if that explanation was not satisfactory, that the Muslims themselves may have committed the atrocities in Ahmici in order to gain international sympathy and that the Muslims were known for doing things like that. I explained to Mr. Kordic that much to my regret, I could not accept any of those explanations as satisfactory in view of the overwhelming evidence to the contrary, and Mr. Kordic with a smile on his face says that he knows that I am not persuaded but he will still try. The meeting ended and I went back to the base and gave my colleague a debriefing, he gave me a debriefing of his interviews that day in Zenica. We discussed further with the British battalion what our evidence had been, tried to get further stories from them and we got, towards the final nights as we became friends with some of the soldiers, yet more stories about atrocities in the region. One soldier had testified that he had been patrolling the region of Ahmici shortly after the attack on April 16th and he had seen a group of HVO soldiers on the road. Another had testified that a group of HVO soldiers were escorting a group of Muslim men, maybe 15 or 20 men, who were clearly prisoners, and when he had asked them what will happen to them, the soldier had indicated in perhaps subtle terms that they were going to be executed. Another soldier who I had met who was at the UNPROFOR garage, which was situated in a different location than the actual UNPROFOR base in Vitez, and which had a very good view of some of the neighbouring hamlets and villages, had mentioned that he himself had seen through his binoculars a group of men being rounded up and executed in a neighbouring village. I could see from the entrance of the garage that it was possible through binoculars to have a very clear and accurate view of some of the neighbouring hamlets and villages. What was interesting is that -- I am not sure if it was that evening or the evening of our last day, which was May 6th, when I was speaking to this particular individual, I believe his name was Sergeant Major Beck, that we saw a number of cars leaving Vitez, I remember there were Volkswagen Rabbit cars, one or two of them, with a group of what happened to be young men in military uniform. They were taking a road, I cannot remember exactly which direction it was, but they were going over a hill to apparently what was a Muslim village behind the hill, behind where we could actually see with our own eyes. Sergeant Major Beck immediately said that was the same group of people who have been going around attacking villages and burning homes. I was very surprised at the certitude with which he made that assertion, but he was proven correct when maybe ten or 15 minutes later over the hill one could see some fires, what appeared to be, if you like, the halo of the fire over the hill and one fire began, then a second, then a third. It seemed as if the fires were being set in a very systematic fashion and it was very clear that homes were being set on fire and that this was really a regular nightly activity. This brought me back to the very first evening when we had arrived, also when we had seen a number of homes being set on fire. Finally, on May 6th, which was the last day for us in the Lasva Valley, there was a high level delegation from the European Community of a British, French and Spanish Ambassador, who wanted to visit the region to try to get a better idea of what had happened in the Lasva Valley and to try and stabilise the situation. We went back once again to Ahmici, this time under very heavy guard. There was an advance team which went to secure the area to ensure that there was no repetition of the incident with the snipers. We once again visited the village. Perhaps the only event which is of significance here was the home that I had mentioned to you earlier that we went to, based on a map which had been drawn by, I believe, Sakib Ahmic or one of the other survivors, which pointed out where the home was where he had been hiding behind the sofa as the home was set on fire and the specific location of the room where the father, mother and two children had been either executed or burnt alive. We went to that home and exactly in the location that we were told, found what were the badly burnt remains of two people who appeared to be adults -- in one case the only parts which we could find were the vertebrae, the pelvis and the skull, and the other parts may have been burnt or decomposed or whatever the case might be. We found also the badly charred remains of what at first appeared to be simply a rag or a carpet or something that had been burnt and these ended up being the body of the four month old infant and the three year old child. We could not determine at that point whether they also had been executed or whether they had simply been burnt alive or whether they had been burnt as the building was destroyed. I should also add that while in Zenica, we also had accounts of the notorious case of the -- what were between four and six women and children who had been hiding in a basement and who had apparently been burnt alive, and apparently the bodies were taken to Zenica and an autopsy had been performed on them, so we ourselves did not see those particular bodies, but we received confirmation that they indeed had -- that this event had indeed transpired. That brings me, your Honour, forgive me for the very extended description of the events, that brings me to the final day May 7th, where we returned to Sarajevo and then subsequently to Zagreb, where we cumulatively put our notes in the form of a report, transmitted it to Geneva where the desk officer, in collaboration with us, drafted the report that I believe you may have before you, the report to the Commission on Human Rights concerning ethnic cleansing by Croat forces in the Lasva Valley region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, the Trial Chamber wishes to thank you for the precision with which you have testified. We are now going to have a 20 minute break, Mr. Prosecutor will certainly have some additional questions to put to you. In cases of testimony of this kind by an expert, the Chamber will appreciate it if those questions will be such that the witness will not repeat what he has already said, but will rather speak in support of the charges contained in the indictment. The hearing is adjourned. We will meet at 11.50. (11.30 am) (A short break) (11.50 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume our hearing. Please have the accused brought in. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you. Mr. Akhavan, I would like to ask you a couple of questions concerning your narrative. The first two relate to the British battalion members that you identified by name, one of which was an individual that you described as Watters, which you were unfamiliar with his rank. Would that be Bryan Watters that you were speaking to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other individual was a Sergeant Beck in the echelon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, the echelon?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The garage. That is the individual who described to you the people going up and lighting fires, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what location did these individuals come from, do you know, town, location? What did Beck say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From where we were situated, I cannot speak about directions in terms of north, south, east or west, but from where the garage was facing Vitez I believe was to our left-hand side down the road, so the cars were moving from Vitez in our general direction. But towards the front of the garage, if you like, there was a road maybe one, at most two kilometres away which came out of Vitez and then went through towards some of the villages behind the hill, which I had mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Sergeant Beck inform you concerning these people and the regularity of their activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had mentioned that there are a group of them and that they had some sort of a leader who was well known for causing problems, and that very often, they would congregate at a certain place in Vitez which could have been possibly a bar where they were drinking together, a restaurant, some other gathering place and that frequently they would have a few drinks, get into their cars and go into a village and abuse people, burn some homes and engage in other such activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have no intention of covering everything in your narrative, but I would like to direct your attention to the meeting where you were talking to Colonel Blaskic on 5th May 1993. You indicated that there was another individual there by the name of Ante Valenta, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could have put on the ELMO Exhibit 80/8 briefly? Is the individual who was at the meeting with you and Blaskic in this picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point to him please on the ELMO, if you could?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be this gentleman with the briefcase and the moustache.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Blaskic indicate in any fashion that when Valenta came into this meeting that he was unwelcome?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apparently not. My impression when Mr. Valenta came into the meeting was that he was very well known. He was, if you like, one of the boys. He just came in really without much introduction, took his seat at the table.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher, we are not going to address that photograph any longer. You mentioned during your meeting with Kordic that he offered you at least two explanations as to those responsible for the atrocities in Ahmici, either the Serbs, or the Muslims might have done it to themselves, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Blaskic offer you any alternative explanation at his meeting with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not believe so. He simply reiterated that he did not know who had done it, but that it was certainly not his soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned likewise that on 6th May you went back to Ahmici to investigate some information that had been given to Mr. Osorio on his trips to Zenica, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President, your Honours, if we may go to a clip, this is a clip coming from Sky News. You have seen this clip of video, have you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are in fact in this video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President, your Honours, if we can show this clip, I think it is about a minute or so. I am not sure of the exact number of this tape, Mr. Dubuisson.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 185. (Videotape played) (Videotape stopped)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As I noted previously, that was you with the helmet and the flak jacket on during the course of that clip, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The British officer who was doing the speaking there, who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the Cheshire Regiment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cheshire Regiment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Likewise after the scene -- it was of Ahmici, that scene, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that scene, there appeared to be a meeting that was filmed where the defendant and others were present, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise any of the people in that meeting, other than the defendant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, well, other than the ECMM ambassadors and Colonel Stewart, I recognise Ante Valenta being present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can move ahead, Mr. Akhavan, to your actual report. You said that you went back to your headquarters and you sent some of your results to Geneva where a report was written, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With your permission, Mr. President, if I can go to the next exhibit, 186, which is the report itself in English and French. (Handed). Before the judges and counsel is the report that was the report drafted by the Commission on Human Rights, dated 19th May 1993. This report was completed long before the international war crimes tribunal for the former Yugoslavia came into existence, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, it came out six days before Resolution 827 was adopted by the Security Council, and certainly at least one or two years before the Tribunal became operational in a meaningful sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to be perfectly clear about this report, there is a section of this report dealing with the city of Mostar, is there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you or Mr. Osorio have anything to do with that portion of this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that portion of the report was primarily done through other sources in Geneva and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without going through every aspect of this report, because the body of it, of course, was attested to during your testimony, what were the conclusions reached by the Commission concerning the events that occurred in Ahmici, Vitez and the surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The basic conclusions which I believe are contained in the latter part of this report, paragraphs 38 to 44, the basic conclusions were that indeed there had been humanitarian law violations committed on all sides in the Lasva Valley region, but that by far the most serious large scale violations had taken place in areas under the control of the Bosnian Croat forces. Then a detailing of some of the -- the nature of some of the atrocities which had occurred, which involves everything from large scale arbitrary executions to torture to sexual assault to deportations, wanton destruction of property, and, of course, the conclusions include the fact that none of the parties, certainly not the Bosnian Croats, had engaged in any form of investigation, let alone Prosecution of those responsible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, after this report was written, was it transmitted to the authorities for the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not certain whether it was specifically sent to Herceg-Bosna, but this was a public document of the United Nations. It was certainly sent to Zagreb and I do know for a fact though that the community of Herceg-Bosna reacted to the report, so one way or another, they did read the report and they did react to it in considerable detail, I would say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just tell the court about their reaction, what they had said that they were going to do or had done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reaction was somewhat muted. I should point out that Tadeusz Mazowiecki was held in very high regard among the Croats, as well as the Muslims, as being one of the few people in the United Nations who had stood up and told the truth with respect to humanitarian law violations, so I think there was some degree of caution in trying to criticise Mr. Mazowiecki, so the criticism is directed at the staff of Mr. Mazowiecki rather than himself. The allegation is something to the effect that the staff are not impartial, that they are clearly biased in their approach and furthermore that they have only had access to evidence of atrocities committed by Croats and not of similar atrocities committed by Muslims, the idea being that since the Croats were very co-operative and civilised that naturally more information would be gathered about atrocities which they had committed. Of course, in reality we had absolutely no co-operation from the Bosnian Croats. As a matter of fact, their snipers tried to kill us when we were trying to investigate, so I think that that is a grossly distorted picture of the situation. They went on to make specific allegations about Zenica, deportations in Zenica, detention in Zenica, and our own report recognises that there have been allegations in Zenica, but because of the very limited amount of time which we had, we basically chose to investigate what had transpired in Vitez and Ahmici, because based on the information which we had, the scale of atrocities were far, far greater than anything which was alleged in Zenica, so there was no question of impartiality, it was really a question of what do you prioritise under the circumstances with very limited resources. There were also some other small points made in the report, something to the effect that the report is inaccurate because it mentions that, for example, Donje Vakuf as being an area where there are hostilities between Croats and Muslims. They point out, correctly, that that was an area which was controlled by the Serbs, so it was only Gornji Vakuf where there was some sort of conflict, so there may have been some very small errors due to the fact that we may have had limited access to information, we may not have had the name of a particular village right, but in any event Donje Vakuf is not mentioned in our report in relation to any atrocities, it is simply mentioned in order to put forward a list of the villages which existed in the area where there were conflicts between Croats and Muslims. In short, the letter of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna suggests that we have been one sided. It does not deny, interestingly enough, that there were atrocities in Ahmici or Vitez. It simply says that: "We do not insist that serious violations of human rights did not occur." They simply say that you should also have taken into consideration what was done against Croats by Muslims. One final thing which I will point out which is amusing is that in the portion of the report called "item", there is a survey, a statistical survey of the population in the region which suggests, for example, that in Travnik, Travnik being the city under government control which was part of canton number 10 in the Vance-Owen Plan and which was to go under Croatian control, although it was predominantly Muslim, according to the statistics offered by Herceg-Bosna, the city was 45.8 per cent Croatian and 37.4 per cent Muslim. In reality, it is the exact opposite, according to the 1991 census, which was conducted still during the days of the SFRY, which indicated that the population of Travnik was 45.3 per cent Muslim and 39.6 per cent Croat, so I think here also there is some propaganda attempt through distortion of statistics to justify the ethnic configuration which existed at that time under the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, did the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna indicate that they had set up any type of commission to look into the facts concerning the crimes in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On two occasions there were some indications. Firstly, when we met with the ECMM people in Zagreb, they had indicated to us that there was an agreement, and I think it was an agreement which was concluded under their auspices and because of pressures which they exerted on the parties, there was an agreement that the parties would investigate the atrocities and to identify those who are responsible, and then once again, in the report sent to Mr. Mazowiecki from Herceg-Bosna. There is a reference I believe on the second page saying that: "Everything that is written in these reports", meaning to say our report, "dealing with crimes in Ahmici was the reason why the HVO formed a commission which is responsible to investigate these crimes." But as far as we know, such a commission, even if it was established, which we never heard any account of, never did any serious investigation, let alone bring anyone to justice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as far as you know, was any soldier or any person ever prosecuted or investigated by this commission, or did you see results of that investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We heard absolutely nothing from the commission. As far as we were aware, the commission existed only on paper and it was clearly a means of appeasing public opinion which was outraged at what had happened in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any indication that any soldier in the HVO was relieved of command or relieved of his responsibilities as an HVO soldier or was court-martialed by the HVO in any way, shape or form?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time, I would, if I have not done it previously, offer into evidence Exhibit 185, which is the video and Exhibit 186 -- I am sorry, 185 is the video and the statement itself is 184 and 184A is the French version of the report of the Commission on Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The report is 184, your Honour? It had been identified as 186.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe I was mistaken, counsel. I believe Mr. Dubuisson corrected the Office of the Prosecutor and the report is 184 and the French version is 184A. So my statements before concerning 186, I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, no objection to 184 if the paragraphs pertaining to Mostar are redacted. I think they are outside the scope of the indictment and I see no point in having the witness cross-examined about them. If paragraphs 26 through 36 are redacted in the document that is filed with the court, no objection to its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is it really necessary for it to be redacted? It seems obvious to me. It is obvious we are not speaking about Mostar, but if you insist on this kind of formality, that these paragraphs be redacted, then we will do so. It just does not seem necessary to me. 184 and 184A will redact paragraphs 26 to 36 which deal with the city of Mostar. Mr. Kehoe, another question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, it is not a question, Mr. President.
