With regard to the actual events of Mostar, of course, there is information concerning Mostar and allegations concerning Mostar in paragraph 5.2 where we note that similar acts have occurred in Mostar. Like the witnesses that we intend to present or stipulate to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 5.2 in the indictment you mean? I am not sure I understand what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, in the indictment. We can redact this information and put it into evidence when we are talking about the widespread and systematic nature of the crimes committed by the HVO when we are talking about Mostar, and we will gladly do that. It seems, Mr. President, that would seem easier to leave it in now and certainly we are not proposing that Mr. Akhavan can answer questions concerning the investigation in Mostar. Nevertheless, it is of some pertinence to the ultimate case to be presented by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is right, Mr. Kehoe. Paragraph 5.2 of the indictment does in fact mention Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, a couple of points. One, I think we would all agree that Mostar was outside of the zone of responsibility of the accused, that is number one. Number two is I will have to check, but it may be this is one of the portions of the indictment that was added by the Prosecution and never submitted to any confirming judge or Trial Chamber. I am not sure of that, I would like to check that. Suffice it to say at this time, this witness cannot speak for this portion of the report and I suggest this portion be offered at a time when it is properly presented with a witness who can verify its contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that the best thing to do would be not to do any redaction for the time being. The transcript will note that Mostar does not fall under the command responsibility of the accused, therefore it need not be dealt with. If the Prosecutor had asked the witness to deal with the question of Mostar, it would be different. Any other comments, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Nor any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We can now move to the cross-examination. Will it be Mr. Hayman? Cross-examined by MR. HAYMAN

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you. Good afternoon, Mr. Akhavan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are a lawyer, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have had some involvement in this case since you have joined the staff of the Office of the Tribunal Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that capacity, have you had occasion to review any witness statements or other documentary evidence collected by the Office of the Prosecutor relating to this investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to 2nd of May 1993, when you went to Ahmici the first time. If we could retrieve, your Honour, Exhibits 51 and 59. They are aerial photographs. Why do we not come back to these subjects when those have been retrieved?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I am sorry, I would need five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, we have agreed that in the future, in principle the Registrar must be told before the beginning of the hearing which exhibits will be required, because Mr. Dubuisson could have found them. We are now at 104, obviously he does not come to the hearing with all hundreds of exhibits. You want to wait a few minutes Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I can come back to this area, your Honour. Regrettably, while I was preparing during the break I was looking for the right number to determine what I would need, so this is not something I knew before the commencement of the hearing. We will return to this, Mr. Akhavan. Let us go forward a day to 3rd May 1993. You went to Zenica on that day, as I recall your testimony. Certain interviews were conducted. Do you know who selected the victims that were presented to you for interview and discussion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not really selected. We went to the war crimes documentation centre in Zenica and they took us to the refugee collection centre, which was really some sort of building or other which housed several hundred, possibly several thousand people. You had all sorts of bunk beds where people slept, so we were simply directed to a room where there were survivors of Ahmici. This was a group of about 100 to 150 people that had recently been released from detention in Dubravica, so we were not -- we did not have individual interviews with individual survivors, we simply had about 50, 60, possibly 100 people in a room and they just came to us one by one and we talked with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, you may address the court, if it please the court. Was your arrival or your trip to Zenica on that day, was that previously arranged with the authorities in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was arranged, I believe, on the same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some period in advance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I think it was possibly -- I do not even think it was arranged in the sense that there was a telephone call or anything, we simply were taken by the British battalion to Zenica to the documentation centre and the idea was that there would always be someone there and then they arranged for us to go to the collection centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you interview any survivors from Ahmici who were males of fighting age, for example between the ages of 20 and 50?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall a single such person who we interviewed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the survivors that you spoke with discuss with you the numbers of Territorial Defence Forces who resided in the village of Ahmici, or is that something that was not discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not discuss it as specifically as you may have mentioned members of the Territorial Defence Force, but we did ask people, not only the survivors but also members of the British battalion whether there was any military presence in the village of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it they told you there was not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They told us the only military presence which could have been would have been, as I mentioned earlier in my testimony, men of fighting age who were on leave to visit their families who may have been in uniform. Another indication which we had about the absence of any significant military presence there was the fact that as far as we know, the Croats had virtually no casualties. There was virtually no resistance to their attack on Ahmici, so all of this led us to conclude that there would have been little, if any, men of fighting age with weaponry in Ahmici at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you determine that the Croats who attacked Ahmici on 16th April 1993 had no casualties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We asked around, we were given no such information. We did not conclude that there was not, but we did not receive any evidence to the effect that there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the Ahmici survivors with whom you spoke on 3rd May 1993, did any of them say that they had seen HV soldiers, that is soldiers from the Republic of Croatia army in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall having anyone say that, no. I do recall, however, members of the British battalion saying that they had seen HV soldiers, not in Ahmici itself but in the region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the specifics of that, where they saw them and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I would have to think about that more carefully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you speak with from the British battalion that told you they had seen HV soldiers in the Lasva Valley or in other environs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had spoken to a number of people, there was not a particular conversation. The understanding was that there were HV soldiers who may have been there in an advisory capacity in assisting the HVO and some of the military experts in particular said that when it came to training for the use of artillery, that HV soldiers, many of them were artillery experts who were training HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify any BritBat soldier who told you that they saw an HV soldier in the Lasva Valley during their tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have a recollection of the particular individuals who I spoke with, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the Ahmici survivors that you spoke with on 3rd May 1993, did they describe the resistance, the armed resistance that did occur in Donje Ahmici on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not recall having heard that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you that there was no armed resistance in Ahmici on 16th April 1993? Is that what the survivors told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends on what is meant by "armed resistance". We were aware that -- people when they are being attacked are not going to simply welcome the people to kill them, that people will resist in any way that is possible. People will pick up shotguns, whatever weapons they had at their disposal and that was the pattern of warfare in that region. In virtually every village, as I mentioned, every man of fighting age was either in an HVO uniform or in the uniform of the Bosnian Serb Army. That was the case throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time. Every fighting age male was mobilised, so what you would have, not only in Ahmici but in other villages, you would have people who were sometimes on leave to visit their family, or in the village for some other reason, who would have a gun and, of course, it was the countryside, many of the people simply had shotguns for hunting, so it is conceivable that a couple of people may have picked up shotguns and tried to defend themselves, but in terms of an organised military resistance in terms of soldiers who have been deployed for that particular purpose and who are able to somehow give some sort of serious resistance to the advancing army, I do not think that there was any evidence, and we did ask the survivors about such evidence and we were not given any indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You are speaking of your opinions and impressions and right now, I am just asking you what you were told on 3rd May 1993 in Zenica. What were you told by the survivors that you spoke with concerning any resistance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think the witness has answered, Mr. Hayman. Perhaps the answer does not suit you, but he has answered your question. He cannot give you more than he has already done so, so pass on to your next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The answer, your Honour, was non-responsive and the record will speak for itself. I will move on. Did any survivor from Ahmici tell you on 3rd May 1993 that the resistance in Donje Ahmici lasted from dawn until nightfall on that day? Did anyone tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that he has asked these questions, he is not satisfied with the answers and he is asking the same question in a different fashion, but it is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Objection sustained. Proceed to your next question, Mr. Hayman, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you had been told that, would that have been a material fact in your report, in the opinions and conclusions you drew in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it would not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think if he was told that, that would be another question, but you keep coming back to the same point. If they had told him, that is a conditional tense. You are even beginning to convey your own opinions, so please put your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will proceed, your Honour, but with all due respect that is how you examine an expert. You have to test his opinions, you have to state possible facts which may be proven true in the course of this trial and if so, this Tribunal should know whether the assumptions the witness made are material to his opinions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: With all due respect that I owe you, Mr. Hayman, I think that the judge who is speaking to you knows also how to question an expert. The Tribunal feels that it is sufficiently informed. You are wasting time, so please go on to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said you learned on this day, you were told that two women, Muslim women were raped while detained after 16th April 1993, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without stating the names, can you tell us, were you told the names of these individuals? If you were, please do not state the names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not recall being told the names of these alleged victims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, and I do not think they would have offered the names. The point is that they knew of two people in their midst who had been taken away and who had subsequently returned and apparently these two people indicated to their neighbours and friends and colleagues that they had been taken away to be raped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you be more specific in terms of where you got this information, who told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were once again some of the survivors which we spoke with in Zenica who had previously been detained in Dubravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to identify them more specifically, the declarants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If I may approach the easel, your Honour, for the photos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you can approach the easel as well. The microphone? We will allow the witness to be able to answer your questions standing, so can it be installed, please? Mr. Dubuisson, the microphone seems to have disappeared, so please let us have this microphone in a corner of the room all the time to avoid wasting time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, from the descriptions on the exhibit list I obviously was not able to identify the correct aerial photograph. I am advised by my learned friend that it is number 50. I regret having to impose on the usher, but I would ask that Exhibit 50 be retrieved and I will return to this area when it is available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. On 5th May 1993, you went to the Hotel Vitez to speak with Colonel Blaskic, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those discussions, did you utilise an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who provided that interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: UNPROFOR British battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the first hour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I may add, I believe there was also an interpreter who belonged to either Colonel Blaskic or the local Bosnian Croats who was also utilised. I am not sure if it was used in this particular case as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who interpreted for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what I am saying, I do not exactly recall, but I do recall there was other than the local interpreter provided by British battalion, another interpreter which worked with the Bosnian Croats, with the HVO themselves, but I do not recall whether both of them interpreted or whether only one interpreted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was present during the first hour of your interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that one or two members of the UNPROFOR British battalion were present. There were one or two other colleagues of Colonel Blaskic, but I cannot recall who they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who was present for BritBat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember the specific name, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall their function or position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall that at all. I could possibly, looking back at my notes, figure out who it was, because there was someone who was assigned to me throughout these days and I would recognise the person actually if I saw him, but the name I cannot recall at the moment, but someone was assigned to me throughout that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct that in the course of this meeting with Colonel Blaskic, he denied ordering the killing of any civilians in Ahmici or anywhere else, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he also deny that he knew in advance that any civilians would be killed in Ahmici or anywhere else, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he also tell you in this meeting that he did not know what had occurred in Ahmici on 16th April and noted that he was not present at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember whether he said that he had no idea, I think he had an idea that there had been hostilities in the region, but to the extent that he may not have known about the details, I informed him on that day all the details of what had happened in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but did he say that with respect to the events you were referencing, the deaths of civilians and so forth, that he did not know what had happened in Ahmici on that day and noted that he had not been there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, no, he did not deny all knowledge. As I said, he had a general impression that there had been hostilities and that there may have been casualties, but specifically he did not admit knowledge of having known that, let us say, 100 or 200 civilians may have been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to look at your statement of June 23rd 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is actually not my statement, it was a statement taken by two members of our office in an interview. I did not at any point sign this statement. For the most part, it is an accurate statement with perhaps one or two small ambiguities which I could resolve for you if you like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you then, the statement in the last paragraph on page 2, in which Blaskic says he did not know, referring to Ahmici, because he had not been there, is that one of the portions of the statement that is correct or incorrect? That is the second line of the last paragraph on page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct if by saying that he did not know we are referring not to the fact that there were armed hostilities in Ahmici and that there could have been casualties; what he did not know specifically was whether there had been large scale civilian atrocities. He did not admit knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say he did not admit knowledge of the details of any atrocities in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to what statement he made to me, yes, it would be fair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you said on direct examination that you concluded that Colonel Blaskic and his subordinates were in control of the HVO in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you base that on Colonel Blaskic's statement to you that he was the HVO commander in the operative zone for middle Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only on that, I based it on the fact that Colonel Blaskic repeatedly told me that the HVO was in firm control of the region. I based it on the fact that he admitted that although there were some paramilitary formations, that they posed no serious threat whatsoever to the control by the HVO of that region, and I based it foremost on the opinion of several members of the British battalion, the Cheshire Regiment, who had spent the past six months on a daily basis surveying the military situation in the Lasva Valley region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Colonel Blaskic tell you that the HVO and the HOS did not get along?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He indicated there were some tensions and that he would keep his distance from the HOS, something to that effect. However, I recall at the headquarters having seen the distinctive black uniform of several members of the HOS who were walking to and fro in the lobby of the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see some black uniformed individuals in the lobby, or did you see a HOS or Vitezovi patch on those individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was also a Vitezovi badge. I remember that the black uniforms did have the familiar Croatian chequered pattern on the arm badge, but in any event, none of the survivors in Ahmici ever said that there was anyone with black uniforms in the village, so there was not much emphasis on HOS in my questions to Colonel Blaskic. It was something I wanted to ask in order to get an indication of whether it would be possible that there was some other military force which was capable of such a large scale and sustained operation without the knowledge, acquiescence, co-operation or control of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your direct testimony that Colonel Blaskic said there was no reason for an attack, no military reason for an attack on Ahmici. Are you confusing your interview with Colonel Blaskic with your interview with Mario Cerkez in that regard? Was it Mario Cerkez that said that and not Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not believe so. I do not even think I discussed the matter of Ahmici with Mario Cerkez because, as far as I recall, strictly speaking he was not responsible for Ahmici. He was strictly responsible for Vitez, but I was distinctly told by Colonel Blaskic -- actually I suggested to him that there were no military targets and he agreed with me, that there was no military presence of any sort. I believe the way in which I posed the question is by asking him whether he thinks there will be any justification for an attack and as far as he had told me, there would have been none, there was no military target or significant military presence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you draft the portion of the report which is Exhibit 184, I believe, which states: "By all accounts, including those of the local Croat HVO commander, this village [Ahmici] contained no legitimate military targets."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which paragraph is that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is paragraph 3 on my copy, which is an Internet copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is paragraph 14 of the official document. Yes, that was -- actually to be very concise, these reports were drafted between Zagreb and Geneva and we were constantly sending drafts back and forth, but the substance of that paragraph is very much based on my observations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you use "local HVO commander" to refer to Mr. Cerkez or Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I referred to Mr. Blaskic. You must recall that the reports are not intended as criminal investigations identifying particular individuals. They are reports which are intended to give the most accurate possible account of the human rights situation in that particular region, so for us, the general term "local Croat HVO commander" sufficed in this case, and we would categorise Colonel Blaskic as a local Croat HVO commander for the purposes of the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In both of your interviews in 1994 and 1995, were you asked to relate what Colonel Blaskic said in your interview with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I do not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In both of your interviews with the Tribunal Prosecutor's investigators in 1994 and 1995, were you asked to relate what Colonel Blaskic said in your interview with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In either interview, did you attribute this statement, that there was no military purpose in attacking Ahmici, to Colonel Blaskic. In either interview, did you attribute that statement to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall, I would have to go back to the text of both my statement and the interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have contemporaneous notes that you could check to be more certain whether it was Mr. Cerkez or Mr. Blaskic that said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have the notes in my possession, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you have them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are possibly somewhere in Geneva, but they are not in my possession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where they are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am not certain. That would have to be done through the Centre for Human Rights, my previous employer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you attempted to retrieve them and obtain them to assist in preparing for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that the staff of the Prosecutor's office have attempted unsuccessfully to retrieve these from Geneva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say your notes are lost? Your notes of your conversation with the accused as far as you know have been lost, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke with him for one hour, one on one, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spoke with him for almost two hours one on one, with some minor interruptions on the part of Mr. Ante Valenta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as you recall his statements, you are recalling those from memory without the aid of your contemporaneous notes, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not specifically correct, because the UN report was based very much on my notes of my discussions with General Blaskic, and with Mr. Kordic, so paragraph 14 is not based on what I remember today, it is based on what notes I had four and a half years ago when the report was drafted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the report --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By reading the report again, four and a half years later, I am in a sense reading my own notes, so I do not think it is accurate to say that I am relying completely on memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Mr. Akhavan, would you not agree that the report has virtually no account in it of your conversation with Tihomir Blaskic on this date in question? There is no account of your conversation with him in the report, is there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was disagree in the sense that -- I would disagree with that, because it was not the practice, and if you read any number of human rights reports which come out of the United Nations system, you will not see a single one which would specifically mention such a meeting. In certain cases, if there is a meeting with a head of state or a government minister or some very high profile individual, in the introductory part of the report, for the information of the audience, there will be a reference, but if these reports were to exhaustively detail the name of each and every individual, then they would become 500 page reports. The whole purpose here is to give a succinct and concise summary to the international community of the human rights situation. That is why we would simply reduce the question to referring to Mr. Blaskic as a local Croat HVO commander. It is, frankly speaking, irrelevant for the Human Rights Commission whether we have spoken with Mario Cerkez or whether we have spoken with General Blaskic. They do not enquire as to the veracity of our claim. The idea is that the special rapporteur and his staff are people of sufficient competence and impartiality that what the Human Rights Commission receives is in reality the result of a quasi judicial process which has considered the evidence for and against the allegations and come to some sort of conclusion. That is the way these reports are regarded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Suffice it to say, your testimony is that you used the report to refresh your memory as to your conversation with Tihomir Blaskic on 5th May 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have asked this question now a third time in a variety of different ways. The witness has answered the question completely, at some length.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Objection sustained. The witness has fully responded to your, I must say, legitimate preoccupations, but you have got your answer so please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You testified in your direct examination with respect to the subject of your knowledge of any investigations or inquiries within the HVO into the atrocities at Ahmici; do you recall that subject?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That subject during my testimony today?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today you have discussed in your direct examination the subject of whether or not you obtained information of any HVO investigation or inquiry into the atrocities in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discuss that subject with Colonel Blaskic on 5th May 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to the best of my recollection I did. I specifically informed him that he was responsible for conducting such an investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was given no indication, either that he was against such an initiative or that he was in favour of it. To the best of my memory, he simply acknowledged what I had told him without giving me any promises or without arguing against me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone else taking notes at your meeting with my client?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was the only person taking notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By this point in time, had you and your colleague developed a list that you referred to of 18 possible perpetrators of crimes in Ahmici on 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that the list was prepared the following day. The first visit to Zenica we wanted to get general information about what had transpired, identity of some of the perpetrators in terms of did or did they not belong to the HVO, what were the circumstances of the attack. During the day, when I was interviewing Colonel Blaskic, my colleague had been in Zenica getting the list of those 18 names, and frankly speaking, we did not have to get the list of particular names, we were not involved in a criminal investigation, but as the UN report indicates, we thought that in addition to helping us than confirm beyond doubt the veracity of the allegations made against the HVO, that we could forward these 18 names to the commission of experts for potential prosecutions at some point in the future, if and when a criminal Tribunal was established, but we did not specifically give those names to -- I did not have those names with me on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you got them the next day, the names, as far as you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got them personally the next day, but my colleague had them on the same day as the interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take any steps to give those names to Colonel Blaskic so that he could use them in an investigation into atrocities in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not, because it was not part of our mandate to engage in such activities. It is not our business as human rights monitors to conduct criminal investigations and to give lists to the authorities in the region. As I said, we haphazardly came across these names. It would have been completely beyond our mandate to give these names, which is why we forwarded them to the appropriate body, that being the commission of experts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I did indicate on subject -- actually during that meeting I did indicate to Mr. Blaskic that we had been given some specific names during our meeting with the survivors in Zenica, although I did not have a list of specific names, just to indicate to him that there were clear perpetrators who came from that region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did anyone else give the list of names to Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to the best of my knowledge. We simply gave them to the commission of experts and I am not aware of what happened after that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described a Mr. Valenta coming into the meeting and making disparaging comments concerning Muslims, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think disparaging is one way of describing it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Colonel Blaskic make any such ethnically disparaging comments towards Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not. He was extremely polite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You have many more questions, Mr. Hayman? My intention is not to limit your cross-examination, it is simply for concern for our lunch break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Only ten or fifteen minutes more, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. In that case, we are going to adjourn and resume work at 2.45. (1.00 pm) (Adjourned until 2.45 pm) 21 22 23 24 25 (2.45 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing resumes now. Please have the accused brought in. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, you may continue cross-examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon. We now have I think the aerial photo that covers the Ahmici area on the easel and I would ask, perhaps with the usher's assistance, that you show us and mark on the transparency that has been placed on top of Exhibit 50 in blue pen, where was the field which I think you described as a killing field, or a field where fleeing individuals were shot and I think you described it as being adjacent or across the road from the Catholic cemetery. If you could tell us and mark in blue in either a square or rectangle, whatever the field was in shape, so we will know exactly what location you are referring to, please. If you could stand slightly to the side so that the court can observe your markings. Thank you. First orient yourself. Do you see the Catholic cemetery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will mark an X.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If that is the most accurate way to indicate, an X that covers the area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will just outline the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A rectangle or trapezoid, whatever would be best.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was roughly this area here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you fill that in, perhaps by marking some diagonal lines across the shape you have drawn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also described in your testimony a ditch or trench or ravine where perhaps 100 or 200 shells had been found. Do you recall that location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly speaking --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me give you, if I may, an orange pen. If you could indicate, pressing darkly against the transparency, the location of that ravine or other depression.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If I may approach, Mr. President? If you could just mark a little bit over that, so that it is clearly marked. Thank you. You also said that around certain houses, 50 or so shells were found. Do you remember what part of the village you saw those houses that had 50 or so shells outside of the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First can you tell us and then we will see if it is useful to mark on this map. Can you perhaps show us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would have to try to visualise how we proceeded through the village, it is actually a bit difficult from an aerial map, but I believe that there were -- we took the road, I believe Vitez should be in this direction, we took the Scimitar and stopped here momentarily and then we I believe took the Scimitar and took the main road up into the village. That is where we began to look at the individual houses, so we did not go from here to look at houses, we just checked here the field and the area where the shell casings were, so I would say that the homes which we saw were roughly speaking in this area (indicates), adjacent to the mosque and possibly a few homes here. This is during our first visit to Ahmici, because on the second day we saw a number of other homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you if you could circle those two areas in red.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course these are only approximations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, you are circling a fairly large area, but you are approximating for the record those areas in which you saw approximately 50 shells outside a number of homes and we can better define that in a moment when you have made your marking. So first you have marked an area around the mosque in lower Ahmici, correct, in a red half circle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, whatever shade this is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the other area where you saw these number of shells was where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that it would have been in this region, although I am not entirely certain, but I will mark it just ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you are marking roughly a trapezoid in middle Ahmici or the Grabovi area, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is no indication that that is the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not know it as such. That is fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just recall that we looked at this area and then we walked up this area and somewhere around here we were attacked by snipers (indicates). At that point we ran back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, do you have any basis to conclude the direction of that sniper fire that came upon you when you were at the higher location in middle Ahmici; was it coming from the high ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that from the impact of the bullets against the wall, on this road, I do not remember exactly where on the road it was, we could conclude that it was coming from this direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just, with a purple pen, draw a big arrow indicating the general direction that you believe this sniper fire came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say it is extremely difficult with any degree of accuracy, because obviously if we had found the sniper, the situation would have changed dramatically. Depending on whether we were in this area or this area, the sniper fire would have come, I will draw a triangle to show the range, something to this effect, it would have come from this direction, from anywhere within this range, I would say. I am not sure how far away they were, but probably the easiest place for them to have shot would have been from the wooded area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more question and I will be done with this exhibit. The shells that you found down in the depression which you have indicated in, I believe, orange; could you tell, do you know, were they shells from rifles or shells specifically from a sniper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not have the expertise to make that determination myself, but the members of the British battalion that I was with told me that those would have been what they would call high velocity bullets which were commonly used by snipers. Frankly speaking, it did not matter much for us to determine what was the exact type of bullets. They were basically two types of bullets, the types which were used by sniper guns or even machine-guns and then there were the much larger casings which were used by anti-aircraft guns, which were frequently used in this kind of combat in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, you may be seated. You described several statements from British battalion personnel to you, you identified one of those speakers as a Mr. Beck. Are you able to identify specifically any of the other speakers who told you some of the specific items which you recounted in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would be able to, of course, speak of my discussions with Colonel Stewart, with Bryan Watters, with Mr. Beck, but I must say that after four and a half years, it is difficult to recount the name of the 15 to 20 people that I spoke with at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it you are not able to match speaker with a particular item of information that you obtained, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After four and a half years, it would be a bit difficult, but I still do remember certain specific items which were of particular interest to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us what those were and matched them with the speakers in your direct examination to the best of your ability?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that I did to the best of my ability. There could be yet other things which I could recollect at a later time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But none that you recollect right now as you sit here, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I did during my testimony point, for example, to Mr. Beck, who gave me some specific information about what he had seen through the binoculars, about what he had told me about HVO soldiers which were involved in burning homes. I recall certain remarks which were made to me by Mr. Watters and Mr. Stewart about who was in command in the region and this was based on their experiences in negotiating cease-fires and in securing safe passage for humanitarian convoys. They indicated to me in unmistakable terms that Dario Kordic and Tihomir Blaskic were the two individuals with whom they negotiated all cease-fires and all cases of securing safe passage for humanitarian convoys in the Lasva Valley on the Bosnian Croat side. There were a number of other soldiers who gave me further details; one soldier who was the commander of a Warrior tank who had indicated to me that he had seen HVO soldiers taking maybe 15 to 20 Muslim men as prisoners, marching away from Ahmici, that was the incident in which, as I explained, after the soldier had enquired from one of the soldiers what would happen to those people, there had been a subtle hint they were going to be executed. There were a number of these small stories which cumulatively gave us the general impression which we developed in this report as to what had transpired in that region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were shown a videotape, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The videotape of our visit to Ahmici village, today?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, you were also shown a videotape of a visit to Colonel Blaskic, with Colonel Stewart then making some statements after the meeting, apparently. It may have been the same videotape, but I am referring to that portion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what occasion that was? Were you present at that meeting with Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As Mr. Kehoe asked me, I was not present at that meeting. That was a subsequent meeting which the European Community ambassadors had with Colonel Blaskic. I had met with Colonel Blaskic only once and that was a day -- it was a day prior to the visit with the European Community ambassadors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do not know what was actually discussed at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No one else has related it to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I may have heard second hand from certain people, but I would not be in any position to give an accurate account of what was discussed. Generally speaking, I believe it was a repetition of the same matters which I had raised, perhaps in addition to other matters which were of concern to the ECMM which, of course, had a broader mandate than we did, but we did have extensive discussions with the ECMM and the three ambassadors prior to the visit to Ahmici, where we debriefed them, where they were very interested in knowing what our findings were and I assume they would have brought those up once again in those meetings, but I have no way of verifying that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the meeting depicted on the videotape was after your meeting with Colonel Blaskic, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of preparing your report and gathering data for the report, did you interview any residents or former residents of the village of Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you interview any residents or former residents of Gacice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We may have, but as I said, it is very difficult to recall, and part of the problem was that after our experience in Ahmici, where we tried to approach the local residents to speak and the sniper fire, we were extremely apprehensive, understandably, from approaching locals. It was only at great risk that we could do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then let me ask a more general question. Other than the Ahmici survivors whom you spoke with in Zenica, did you go to any villages other than Ahmici or any other locations and speak to villagers from any other villages in the Lasva Valley that you specifically recall and can tell the court about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did go to Miletici, as I explained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excluding Miletici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but we made a trip there in particular because we wanted to see some Croats who may have suffered violations at the hands of Bosnian Muslim forces. We had a number of displaced persons who had congregated around the UNPROFOR base, so we met a large number of people not in their own villages which had been burnt or destroyed and, of course, it would have been useless for us to go to those villages, because there was nobody there. We did drive through several villages where there had been extensive destruction, but the village, I do not know the name you said, Gacice, which you mentioned, I do not recall, once again, so many years later, but I do believe that we had a number of displaced persons who had come seeking the protection of UNPROFOR and awaiting their relocation by UNHCR who had been from a village which had been recently attacked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You think that was Gacice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I forget -- actually I believe that there was a television camera which recorded their arrival, one of the men had been shot in the arm by one of his neighbours and I believe that UNPROFOR had tended to his wound and given first aid and there was some sort of coverage. Perhaps there is some mention there, but I do not remember the specific village. We had hundreds of villages which we looked at in different regions of Bosnia. It is very difficult to remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the extent of your recollection on that issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the time being, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to Stari Vitez on 4th may 1993, tell us about the fortifications and the BiH army presence that you saw there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not see specific fortifications, but in general there were roadblocks and there were people on roof tops with weapons. I do not recall having seen anything along the lines of an armoured vehicle or a tank or an artillery piece. For the most part, there were simply men with weapons, and the key roads were blocked, sometimes with burnt out -- shells of burnt-out cars simply to block the road, but in terms of weaponry, there was simply rifles, guns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you estimate how many armed men you saw in Stari Vitez on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult to give an account of the situation throughout Stari Vitez. We were at two locations, both locations on the border with the Croat controlled areas and I would say that at each of those locations, there were not in excess of ten people with rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of preparing your report, did you interview any officers or soldiers of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually we did speak with certain officers who were just ordinary -- the sort of soldier which I referred to earlier, who was simply in his own village with his own family. We drove to a number of places, the names of which I cannot recall, isolated hamlets and villages, where some of the Bosnian Muslim soldiers gave us their account of the situation in the region. I remember going to one place which had been the subject of artillery bombardment, I forget where it was. It was maybe two or three kilometres away from Vitez. We did also speak with a Bosnian army commander, a more senior commander, who had come to the -- not to the UNPROFOR base but to, I believe, the ECMM office which was adjacent to the UNPROFOR base in order to hold negotiations with some HVO counterparts, with respect to a cease-fire, release of hostages, and so forth. That was another occasion during which we spoke with a Bosnian army officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you specifically discuss with any BiH army personnel their presence in the Lasva Valley, where they had brigades, where they had headquarters, where they had units et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the matter was raised. Most of the information that we got was from UNPROFOR and we did ask UNPROFOR about Bosnian army positions. I think that that was the more credible source. We realised that whether we were getting information from the HVO or Bosnian army sources, that the information, we would treat it with some degree of suspicion. But they did tell us they felt very cheated, if you like, betrayed about these attacks, because they were very weak in that area, they really had no military presence in the area, they were all deployed elsewhere on the front-line with the Serbs and that really what had happened in Ahmici, Vitez, was, in their own words, "an easy kill" by the Bosnian Croats, an easy way to grab land without really taking any significant casualties. From the events which transpired after that date, it became clear when the Bosnian army began to advance in that region that they had to redeploy armed forces from other areas where they were being used to fight Bosnian Serb armed forces, against the HVO in order to be able to push back the Bosnian Croats and to occupy some of those areas, but that was the general impression which we had of their military presence in the region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the BiH army personnel you spoke to did not give you any further details than what you have stated concerning their presence in the Lasva Valley, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not give us further details and we were not prodding for further details, as we were not prodding the HVO for further details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you review any BiH army documents in preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you review any HVO documents in preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no one really volunteered them to me. I had asked Mario Cerkez if I could have some situation reports from April 16th and he sort of suggested that he may give it, he may not give it, but in the end, there was really no indication that that would be forthcoming, but we did request from Mr. Cerkez to receive certain documents, but in the end we did not receive anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask Colonel Blaskic for anything that he did not provide you with in connection with your interview with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not ask Colonel Blaskic specifically for any documents. As I said, at that point in time we had accumulated so much evidence and testimony that my meeting with Colonel Blaskic was really to give him an opportunity to state his case, to explain to us where and why we may have erred in arriving at our conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you received no co-operation in your inquiry from the Bosnian Croats. Then I take it you do not include Colonel Blaskic in that, insofar as he gave you a two hour interview and you have said you did not ask him for anything he did not provide, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Co-operation exists at different levels. It was very kind of Colonel Blaskic to agree to meet with us, as it was with Mr. Kordic, but in reality, I believe that is the absolute minimum which could be expected under the circumstances. Certainly our experience in Ahmici and other places was that the Bosnian Croats were not at all happy with us snooping around, getting evidence of atrocities which had been committed. There was really what I would consider to be the minimal possible co-operation under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did not ask him for any further co-operation, at your meeting with the accused, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, with respect to the investigation and punishment, specifically say that it was his responsibility to conduct an investigation, and it was his responsibility to ensure that those members of his -- those who were his subordinates who had committed these crimes should be brought to justice and I did request that we be kept apprised of such developments and we had subsequently further communications with the Herceg-Bosna authorities in that regard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In regard to investigation and punishment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in regards to, "what have you done, anything, about Lasva Valley? Have you done anything about Mostar? Have you done anything about a number of other cases", which we were investigating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you speak with concerning whether "anything had been done" regarding the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not do the subsequent investigations on Mostar. I was deployed to investigate the situation in Eastern Slavonija and Krajina, so I would have to refer you to those of my colleagues who had made those subsequent missions, but I do recall during our discussions, our daily meetings in headquarters at Zagreb, hearing that this matter had been pursued further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The report was published, you said that certain individuals in Herceg-Bosna or somewhere were critical of the report. First of all, can you tell us, do you know whether Colonel Blaskic was given a copy of the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of any criticism from him regarding the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the mass grave in Stari Vitez, 100 or 101 bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say that it was in Stari Vitez, it was in Vitez, that is 101 people were buried, but I am not aware of the location of the grave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it may be in Stari Vitez, you are just not sure, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may be, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you informed that those bodies came principally from Ahmici, but also from other parts of the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, was I told?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told that specifically the Muslim bodies came principally from Ahmici and to a lesser extent from other locations in the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not told that. I know that a lot of the bodies were taken from Ahmici to Zenica, because there was a morgue in Zenica where many of the survivors also could have access to these bodies. As far as the origin of some of those who had been killed, the impression which I was under is that most of them were from Vitez itself, but clearly there is a possibility that some of them could have come from neighbouring villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your impression was that close to 95 Muslims were killed during the 16th April conflict in the immediate environs of Vitez and Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That appeared to be the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Beck of BritBat told you about the individuals in the two cars who it appears went off and started some fires. Did he identify for you the unit or the leader of the unit that those individuals belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did he describe that unit or those individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were a group of young men, soldiers from Vitez. They were not described as a paramilitary unit, they were HVO soldiers apparently, from what he had told me, but they were particularly notorious for doing a lot of dirty things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is what Mr. Beck told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His job was in the garage, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He did not leave the base in the course of his duties, he stayed in the garage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sure he left the base in the course of his duties. I do not think there is anyone who would just sit in the garage all day, certainly not him. Clearly his job was to guard the garage. He was not a technician, he was not changing spark plugs, he was a military officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would offer the transparency which is on top of Exhibit 50 and I believe it is the next in order, D72?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, that is D72.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So this transparency will have D72 on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Akhavan. That concludes my examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayman. Mr. Kehoe, have you any additional questions you wish to ask, remaining, of course, within the scope of the cross-examination. Re-examined by MR. KEHOE

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Mr. Akhavan. By the time you published this report or at least when you left the Lasva Valley area on 7th May 1993, had you had a complete count of individuals dead and individuals missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely not. If anything, it was a very preliminary count.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple of questions that came up during cross-examination and you noted, when Defence counsel was cross-examining you concerning the unsigned statement of 23rd June 1995, that you saw this past Saturday, you said there was something inaccurate in that and did not follow up on that. What were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think on page 4 there is one sentence which I think misrepresents or slightly distorts the statement which reads: "I do not think that Blaskic would have had the intelligence to plan an attack but Kordic would have had the knowledge".

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Beyond the scope, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I did not hear what you had to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The question is beyond the scope of the cross-examination. He is going into some other area, some other part of one of his statements that was not enquired of at all in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, would you go to the end of your question first before we can decide on whether it should be answered or not. I would like to understand what the question is that you are asking. I want to understand it before knowing how to rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. In response to a question in cross-examination, the witness stated, when he was being questioned from this statement of 23rd June 1995, that there was something inaccurate in the statement, and that he offered to explain the inaccurate portion of the statement if given the opportunity. Mr. Hayman at that juncture went on to the next question and I am just merely picking up from his answer, saying tell the court that which you think in this statement is inaccurate. That is all I am asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You have to say, however, that Mr. Hayman did not go all the way to the end of his question. Let us not open up a Pandora's box. Since the question was not asked, maybe he forgot, I do not know if he forgot or not. Let us move to another question, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can I ask that question, of that which is in the document is inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, there is no point, since the question was not asked completely. Why do you want to create an incident about one of Mr. Hayman's objections since he did not ask the question. Yes, this goes beyond the scope of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Excuse me. (Pause). You were asked some questions concerning the report and if I might turn specifically, Mr. Akhavan, to page 4 in the English version, paragraph 14. In that paragraph, you noted that the local Croat HVO commander stated that Ahmici contained no legitimate military targets. In response to questions by Defence counsel, you said that this was Blaskic that said this and not Cerkez, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also stated, did you not, that just referring to the local commander was just a reference for the purpose of this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How in paragraph 14 -- let me withdraw that. In paragraph 12, did you refer to any local HDZ leader as a, "local member of the Croatian Democratic Union"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is in mid paragraph 12?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that say, "a prominent local member of the Croatian Democratic Union suggested on the radio, without any apparent justification, that a massive attack by government forces was imminent." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is this prominent local member of the Croatian Democratic Union?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That refers to Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you said at the outset of your testimony that Dario Kordic is a Vice-President of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the HVO. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Akhavan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to clarify some of your statements for my own knowledge. When you made a reconstruction or a construction of the attack on Ahmici, I noted that you mentioned that there was mortar shelling in the northern part of the village, in front of every house there was ammunition, largely used, there was anti-aircraft guns and shellings and so on. Then you added also that the operations, either there or elsewhere, required great preparation. Would that entail that it could only be done by organised forces -- or could it be done by separate amateurish gangs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were a number of factors which led us to believe that it was an organised operation. For one thing, the use of mortars, rocket-propelled grenades and other such semi-heavy weaponry suggested that it could not have been let us say a band of just a few people carrying guns, ordinary guns. The amount of ammunition that was used was also quite significant, and because of the logistics of the village and the expert opinion which we had from members of the British battalion, they estimated that on average it would have taken about 100 soldiers to engage in such an operation. The scale and extent of the destruction led us to believe that it would have been very difficult simply for a group of rogues who may have been drunk to attack the village, to inflict such considerable damage, to kill so many people, to systematically burn each and every Muslim house in the village, and also, based on the sequence of events of the shelling which occurred in the northern part of the village, of the killing field where about 20 people had been ambushed, all of this suggested some degree of co-ordination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All these areas were under Croatian control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, the HVO was clearly the dominating force in that region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your interview with General Blaskic, he told you that he was in charge of that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic denied that the HVO soldiers could have committed that and told you it was by Serbs who infiltrated or Muslims who wanted to commit this so that in the eyes of the world they would be victims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic suggested that explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You said there were 50 or 60 survivors who were able to identify the perpetrators. Did they identify any Muslims among them or any Serbs among them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not believe so. They informed us that they were all Croats from Ahmici and neighbouring villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned also that, if I understood rightly, one of the soldiers, that he could see through his binoculars the execution which was taking place, and you indeed were able to check that it could be done, to see through the binoculars the executions or the place where it was done.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have binoculars with me at that point, but I could even without binoculars see that it was possible to see the village, it was maybe half a kilometre away, and it was possible to see the houses, to see the street. It was possible to see people even in the village, but I did not specifically check with the binoculars to see what could have been seen. I imagine that it would have been possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did he further tell you that he saw who was executing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that he did not. He could simply -- what he said is that he could simply identify them as being local soldiers, he could not identify specifically who they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he could see they were soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned I think that from 200 houses in Ahmici, 20 only were undamaged.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they by any chance Croat houses or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apparently I think there were, they were local Croats who were from Ahmici itself. It was the home of the Croats in Ahmici which were not damaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because in another statement you mentioned that every form of life was being destroyed, including the livestock.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which means there was no discrimination in the killing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that it was the Muslims of the village and their property which was the object of the attack. There were still several Croat families who were living in the village and it appeared from everything that we saw that they were going about their lives as they would on a daily basis. They had their clothes' line with wet laundry hanging and they were walking about the village doing their business. I do not recall if there were any -- if there was any livestock remaining in the village. One of the things that we were a bit perplexed about is why they had killed the livestock, rather than stealing it for themselves, but there were very few live animals remaining in the village at that point in time, a few stray dogs perhaps, a few horses maybe some cows, but there were a large number of carcasses all over the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there, to your knowledge, any revolt on the part of the Muslims which provoked this military reaction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not describe it as a revolt. There were clearly some tensions in the region, going back several months. I believe that there had been certain tensions because of the Vance-Owen Plan and the way in which the ethnic boundaries had been drawn. A few days earlier Mate Boban, I believe, had been in Travnik and there was an attempt to raise the flag of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna to stake their claim to Travnik and that had resulted in a shooting incident. There were a lot of tensions between the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats, as to who should be ruling that area. I think that tension spilled over into isolated acts of violence, including some cases in which members of the various armed forces were taken hostage, for example, but I do not believe that the residents of Ahmici themselves were about to rebel or were somehow arming themselves and preparing for some sort of military operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were mainly civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Overwhelmingly, from what we could tell. There could have been maybe a handful, literally three or four people, but as I said, we do not certainly have complete information, but every indication we have is that there was no outside military presence in Ahmici on the part of the Bosnian Muslim. If there was any military presence, it would be the sort of soldier on leave which I described to you. The soldier at home with his family who may have a gun there, or it could have been local people who as country people they had shotguns very often they would go hunting. That is the only kind of resistance I think there would have been. Of course, even if the village was destroyed and a lot of civilians massacred, it is conceivable that many of these people may have gone into hiding and may have still tried to resist, that could have carried on for several hours, but the actual destruction of the village and the killing I think could have been achieved possibly in half a day, with about 100 people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad. I turn to Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, just a few questions which I shall put to you by way of clarification. You were speaking of Ahmici and you told us that there were about 200 houses, 180 of them were destroyed, but about 15 to 20 were not. Are you in a position to help the Tribunal by saying whether you had any information as to who owned those 15 to 20 houses which were not destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The information was largely what we received from the British battalion, because we were not in a position to independently confirm who the owners of those houses were.
