As I explained when we tried to approach one of the locals, the sniping incident took place and made it virtually impossible. I was told by certain people that there were certain architectural distinctions between Croat and Muslim homes, but I believe that is somewhat artificial, because there were many people who were living in each others' homes, property was exchanging hands either through commercial transactions or through displaced people taking over other people's homes. So that was the only information which we really had from the British battalion and also our own logical conclusion based on the accounts of all the survivors, that is basically all the Muslims who could have left without being killed had basically left, that there was no one remaining there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anyone in those houses which were not destroyed, in or around them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We saw, as I explained, one old lady with her two grandsons. We saw that a number of the homes had, as I said, laundry which was out to dry and the homes were really unscathed, not a single bullet mark. We saw on the occasion when we came with the European Community ambassadors, an elderly -- not an elderly man, an older man who was walking through the village, so clearly there were people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me a little about the anti-aircraft shells. You are not a military man. How did you recognise those shells as anti-aircraft shells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is one of those things that you learn as you go along and I relied on the expertise of my friends in the British battalion, but in general, an anti-aircraft gun has a much bigger casing than a bullet coming from a rifle, and I would say that an anti-aircraft casing would be anywhere from two to three times larger. We are talking here about that bronze coloured or brass coloured casing which is left behind after the bullet is fired, so it was quite easy to make that distinction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those shells in the vicinity of the houses? How near to the houses were those shells fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall if those specific shells were around the houses or around the -- or in some parts of the road, because presumably an anti-aircraft gun would be something not so mobile as a rifle or a machine-gun, so it could be that they had laid it somewhere and they were just firing the gun randomly throughout the village. The casings which we saw around the homes were largely coming from rifles or machine-guns, they were the smaller casings, not anti-aircraft casings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do forgive me, I have asked the question because of a layman's impression, which possibly is erroneous, that an anti-aircraft gun is only intended for long distance firing. That is not correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct that an anti-aircraft gun is not intended for such operations, but what we saw in many cases, and as I spent more months in Bosnia-Herzegovina I saw time and again, weapons which were being used in inappropriate terms. We had also cases in Krajina where anti-aircraft guns were being used in attacks on villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me something else. I think it was on 1st May that you were taken on an outing in one of these vehicles and you peered through the peep holes and you said you saw some men in military uniform looting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Tribunal what kind of uniform those men had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From a distance, it was not possible to look specifically at their arm badge. From what I recall, they had the typical camouflage uniform of military men, a sort of brownish grey uniform, but I could not look specifically at their armbands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that same day I think, or the day before, I am not sure, you saw some houses on fire.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see flames?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or just smouldering material?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, flames, very large flames coming out of the doors and windows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you saw flames, could you give us an impression of the estimate you yourself might have made as to how long before those fires were set?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My own impression and the impression of the soldiers in the tank was that the flame would have been set maybe half an hour before, 15 minutes. It was quite new, you could tell that the smoke had not yet completely stained the white facade of the walls on the outside, and that much remained to be burnt in the house, so to say. The flames were still quite vigorous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are telling the court that the process of destruction continued after 16th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Definitely yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us turn to your two hour conversation with General Blaskic. You told him something to the effect that you thought it was his responsibility to investigate and punish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he deny or accept your suggestion that it was his responsibility to investigate and punish?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not specifically accept or deny that it was his responsibility. What he did say, however, is that it was not his soldiers that had committed these crimes and my sense was, it was only my sense, that by implication he would not be responsible because it was not his soldiers who had committed these crimes, but at no point did he say either that he was going to investigate the matter or that he was not, he simply did not make any remarks, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I was not very clear. I did not intend to ask you whether he said that he intended or not to investigate. My question concerns this: did he accept or reject your proposition that it was his responsibility to investigate what had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, your Honour, neither.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that you indicated to the court that he took the position that Ahmici was an area within his military responsibility, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you gather that he was aware of what had happened in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I gathered based on the proximity of Ahmici to his headquarters which was maybe two kilometres down the road and based on extensive destruction of Vitez itself, it was really incredulous to believe as a military commander that he would not have been apprised of what was happening two kilometres down the road. I also was under the impression that he has certainly some idea at the least that there had been some sort of hostilities in Ahmici. I do not believe he denied knowledge of that. What he denied knowledge of was that a large number of civilians may have been victimised, and, of course, I proceeded to inform him in detail what we had discovered and seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say whether or not he had visited Ahmici since the events which took place on 16th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what I recall, he said that he had not visited Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say whether he intended to visit Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall him making any comments in that regard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask him whether he proposed to visit Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not believe I formulated it in those terms. I formulated it in terms of -- I do believe that I may have suggested perhaps in a rhetorical fashion that he should definitely go and see for himself what had happened there, but in more specific terms, what I -- I do not think it would be accurate to say I requested it of him. Perhaps I informed him that he was responsible to conduct an investigation; whether conducting an investigation involves that he personally make an on site visit or not is something which I did not really feel it was within my prerogative to comment on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us turn a little to the HOS. You said you saw elements of the HOS in the lobby of the Vitez hotel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, and subsequently I learned that although they were still known as HOS by certain people because of their black uniform, they were actually most probably the Vitezovi, rather than the HOS. HOS, I believe, was the paramilitary formation in Croatia which had been involved in the hostilities against the Krajina Serbs, and the Vitezovi, to the best of my knowledge, was related to but not necessarily the same as HOS, but I am not exactly sure about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My impression is that you said that he indicated there was some measure of tension between himself and the HOS. Is that a way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he take that as far as to suggest that he was not in control of any military operations which the HOS might conduct within the area of his command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I left the meeting with the distinct impression, reinforced several times by Colonel Blaskic, that he was the military commander and he was the one who was making the decisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw Vice-President Kordic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And spoke with him for about 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was in uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What uniform was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are speaking about the particular arm badge which he had, I do not recall. All I would remember was that he was wearing the typical camouflage military uniform. I do not know whether it was specifically an HVO uniform or whether it was something that he liked for fashion purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then we shall leave that there. I turn to your statement to the effect, I believe, that the happenings at Ahmici were a matter of some public interest; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very much so, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were reports circulating in the media and on TV about what had happened at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were many reports, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, if I recall your testimony correctly, there was no international criminal court established to deal with events taking place in that area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But were there calls in the media for the establishment of such a court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there had been certain calls and there had been missions previously, one of them was a mission I myself had been involved in with the CSCE which had suggested the establishment of such a court and there were others calling for it as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, the suggestion that such a court should be established was made by the interim report of the committee of experts which was filed, I think, on 9th February 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, sir. I believe that earlier on, Tadeusz Mazowiecki had also made a recommendation to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a resolution of the Security Council of 22nd February had in fact promulgated a decision to establish an international criminal court for the purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Tribunal was later set up on 25th May of that year.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the framework within which your visit took place during the first week of May 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Definitely not, sir. The mandate of the special rapporteur was clearly to look at the question of state responsibility and the absence of a normally functioning state to look at the responsibility of the parties to the conflict for atrocities. At no time in any of our reports, whether against the Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Muslims or Bosnian Serbs, did we specifically mention even the most notorious names, such as those of Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic, instead we had this standard formulation of leaders, people in positions of authority, because it was not really the business of our special rapporteur to delve into such matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I misled you. I did not intend to ask you about the purpose of your mandate. I merely intended to ask you about the general framework within which your particular visit to the area occurred during the first week of May, that there was talk of setting up an International Criminal Tribunal to deal with specific violations of international humanitarian law in the area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. Perhaps I have not understood entirely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that proposals to this effect had been engaging the public interest and had been presented in the media, including television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, but they were met at the time with great scepticism, your Honour. I think that to that effect, I am not sure to which extent the potential establishment of such a court, even on paper, let alone its becoming operational, was something very tangible at that point in time for many of us, although we greatly desired its establishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, many questions have been asked. I would like to ask something for my own information as well, very quickly. You spoke about the hamlet of Miletici, perhaps I am not pronouncing it correctly, and that there were Mujahedin there, but as you also connected this with a question of reprisals, I would like to know whether in your opinion these Mujahedin existed there before the attack, or if they had come in order to respond to a threat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the attack on Ahmici, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was not specifically thinking about Ahmici, but you had spoken about them when you were referring to the hamlet of Miletici. You spoke of Mujahedin who had been recruited by the local population who were a sort of mercenary who were to respond to torture and atrocities committed by the other party. These Mujahedin, were they an isolated element here? Do you have the impression that this territory was one on which several weeks earlier, because they thought there would be an attack, that the Mujahedin had come or did they come after the first attacks, the first threats? That is my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The so-called Mujahedin were somewhat of a mystery, your Honour. No one really knew exactly what their relationship was with the former Bosnian army. There were those who suggested they were part of a so-called Seventh Brigade, others who suggested that they are really a loose cannon, that really no one controlled them and they did their own thing. They were composed partially of local Bosnians and partially of foreign mercenaries or volunteers. As to your question, it is difficult to tell to what extent the killing in Miletici was an act of vengeance for what has transpired in Vitez, Ahmici and other areas, and to what extent these people were simply local criminals who had sized the occasion to engage in some sort of brutality, which was an unfortunately common occurrence in the war where people for their own ends would seize the opportunity. But we were told by one of the elderly Croats in the village who I believe had some sort of relation to one of the young men who had been decapitated, that one of the people who had come to the village along with some foreign looking, people speaking foreign languages, lived just down the road and he even pointed out the home of the person. There was some suggestion that this man may have been a bit of a gangster. They said he had some nice cars and he was involved in all sorts of business practices, so the impression which we gained is that there was one man who lived literally less than a kilometre away from Miletici and that he may have brought with himself one or two mercenaries. We were also told that the one or two Bosnian army officers who either lived in or around the hamlet would normally protect them, but that in this case, they had not themselves participated in the attack, but they had simply not reacted, perhaps in collusion with the attackers or perhaps out of fear, we do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were about to carry out one of your first inspections (not interpreted). At some point in your mission, at the very beginning, I noted that down, you were fired on. Do you remember you said that? Later on, when you met the accused, you spoke to him about that, the fact that you were shot at, which was very dangerous. Did you possibly speak to him and if you did, what was his answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did mention to the accused that we had been fired upon and that we took, of course, great exception to any attempt to impede our investigation, and I mentioned that we had very clearly marked UN helmets and flak jackets and armbands such that there could have been no misunderstanding as to who we were, and as far as I know, the accused did not offer any explanation as to who may have committed the crimes, because I myself suggested clearly that it could not have been anyone except the local HVO who were in control of the region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps this refers back to questions that my colleagues asked, and if so I ask your indulgence. In light of the conversations which you had, among others, with the accused and the presence of Dario Kordic or Valenta, did you have some idea of the hierarchy among those men? I am not speaking about what you learned afterwards, you learned many things about that hierarchy, but I am trying to put myself in your place at the time those conversations took place. You had a conversation with the accused, then you saw Mr. Valenta going by, you met with Mr. Kordic. I have a twofold question. Were you able to get an idea of the command structure at that time? Also, could you distinguish what was political and what was military, the military person, was he also involved in politics and did the politicians limit themselves to politics? Could you answer those two questions, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I had a general idea, during the first two days especially of my visit there as to who was running the show. This was based in large part on the experiences of the UNPROFOR commanders and UNHCR and other officials who either had to negotiate cease-fires or who had to negotiate safe passage for humanitarian convoys or for displaced persons to be able to leave out of that area safely, to go, for example, to Zenica, where they would gather in the collection centres. In all cases, I was told that -- if I may add, it was a bit difficult in the context of the armed conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina in general, and in the particular case of Herceg-Bosna, to draw a clear line of separation between military command and political authority. The two seemed to have a very integrated relationship to one another. I was told that Dario Kordic was really the most serious power broker in the Lasva Valley region, being second only to Mate Boban --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not interested in what you were told, I am sure people told you many things. I want to know whether during the meeting you could see very quickly who was the person who was most pre-eminent, who was the one who was giving orders. Was it this one or the accused who is doing it? This is the impression I am trying to get at. I know you know the rest or at least you have an idea about the rest. I would like to know what you felt at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Based on my subjective impressions, which is what you are asking me, your Honour, my impression was that Dario Kordic was the mastermind, if you like. He was the ideologue, he was extremely sophisticated and if I may add, without being impolite, somewhat sly in the sort of explanations he was offering and what he was trying to persuade me of. My encounter with Colonel Blaskic was, I would say, quite different. I found that he was much more low key and obliging; not in the sense that he was willing to co-operate in divulging information, but that he was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you talking about Blaskic now? I am sorry. I think first you spoke about the ideologue, somewhat sly in your words, that was Dario Kordic, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now we agree we are talking about Blaskic, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My impression was that Colonel Blaskic was less of a political mastermind and more of a military executor, if you like. I was not under the impression that Colonel Blaskic was a purely military, in the sense that he had no involvement whatsoever in the bigger agenda of the HDZ political party which was really a one party state in Herceg-Bosna, which controlled virtually all aspects of politics and military in the region. So there was an impression that they were co-operating very closely in what was evidently a relatively small geographical area, a very small and, forgive the expression, incestuous community of political and military leaders, who were constantly meeting and discussing things with one another. There was no sense they were isolated, but there was the sense that Kordic would be the one who would have the overall theory, if you like, of what the political objectives of Herceg-Bosna should be and Blaskic would be more the sort of person who would implement as a military man, which he was, a professional soldier, the policies which were conceived by someone such as Kordic and further away by Boban in Mostar. That is just my subjective impression, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to speak about the report, not yours but the second one, that is Exhibit 184A, in French. You did not draft that, but you said that large parts of what you had observed had been printed in it, without being the author itself. Could we say that paragraph 43 could explain to us something, that is the first sentence. I will read it in French: "The Peace Plan pursuant to which Bosnia-Herzegovina would be divided according to ethnic boundaries was used in order to set up homogenous ethnic zones." In the mind of the person writing this, which to some extent you may have contributed, do you make a connection between the events which took place in the Ahmici area and this Peace Plan? Was it something which was just set up in order to have a plan, or was it something really specific? Would you explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I should add first of all that the conclusions portion of not only this report but all of these reports is where Prime Minister Mazowiecki had the greatest say. He was obviously not in the position to do the investigations on the ground, that is where he relied on us, but his role was largely to draw conclusions and make recommendations. It must be remembered that this report came at a time when there was intense political debate about the wisdom of ethnic partition in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Mr. Mazowiecki was one of the leading critics of such a policy. Not to say that we did not agree with his observations in this respect, but we did not draft specifically that paragraph. The impression which we gained on the ground was that the parties were trying to resolve the question of the ethnic partition of Bosnia on the ground, while at the same time there were political negotiations going on in Geneva and elsewhere. All the parties were trying to create the best possible ethnic configuration so they could present their ethnic domination in a certain area as a fait accompli. Unfortunately this was part and parcel of the armed conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, something which I think anyone who had any familiarity with the situation on the ground would not deny. There was an impression that the canton number 10, which I had mentioned earlier in the Vance-Owen Plan, which eventually was scrapped for a different sort of partition, had created tremendous tensions between the Croats and the Muslims who were now vying for power. The Croats felt they should already begin to execute the Vance-Owen Plan by asserting their dominance. As I explained, there was the incident where the Croat flag was raised in Travnik which created many tensions. To which extent there was a direct correlation from the territorial demarcation of the plan and the attack in Ahmici I am not entirely certain, but everything we looked at led to the conclusion that this was seen as a means of pre-emptively implementing that partition and there were, according to many well-informed sources who we spoke with, many political statements which had been made almost immediately prior to April 16th. In one case even I believe the ultimatum which had been given, that by April 15th all Muslim forces should be disbanded and the domination of Herceg-Bosna in this canton must be realised or else there was going to be some sort of reprisal, or whatever the case might be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a last question I would like to ask you. When you met General Blaskic, after having made the comments about which we do not have to speak again, that is regarding his responsibility as a local HVO commander in respect of the atrocities that had been committed in Ahmici, after all of this, I would like to ask you whether at any point during the conversation, he said to you that he had given orders, taken decisions, that is command orders, headquarters orders, reminding his troops, the HVO troops, that they had to respect the laws and customs of war and the Geneva Conventions, or respect for protected peoples. Did he say to you, "yes, I understand what you are saying", or, "no, I am not responsible, no, I am not aware of this", or might he have added, for example, "in any case in my military orders I also state that certain international humanitarian laws had to be respected", or did he not say anything at all about it? That is what my question is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not believe that any specific statements were made. If I may share with you once again my somewhat subjective interpretation of the meeting, I believe that the statements made by Colonel Blaskic indicated some degree of unease and at the same time evasiveness. I repeated certain questions several times and each time Colonel Blaskic repeated the same answer which did not really answer my question. I do not think at any point he tried to be defiant and to say that, "we are not going to co-operate", nor did he at any point indicate that he would take any action or assume any responsibility. He repeated simply that he is in control of the region and he is in control of his soldiers and that his soldiers had not committed such a crime and would not commit such a crime. At no point did he answer the specific question of who may have been responsible, whether he was going to take any action, whether in the form of instructing his soldiers not to repeat such crimes again or in the form of investigations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. You already said that. No, I wanted to know whether he might have said to you, "I am a soldier, I am a leader and I am concerned with the Geneva Conventions. Here are the orders that I give to my troops and I say in those orders that they must always be careful because any soldier that would not respect these conventions or the laws of war, I have given this or that order on this or that day and I am concerned with this". He could have said to you, "I do not always know what is going on in my area of responsibility but I am concerned about it and I give orders"; that did not happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nothing with that degree of specificity was mentioned to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have no further questions, but I turn again to my colleagues. Judge Riad has several other questions I would like to ask you. Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, in your last summing up, you mentioned that the Vance-Owen Plan initiated people to -- initiated the parties to pre-emptively implement the partition; in other words, to actualise the ethnic configuration. Could you be more clear about that? What do you mean by the "ethnic configuration"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Vance-Owen Plan was based on the idea of ethnically based cantons. The idea was that Bosnia-Herzegovina would be carved up into a series of cantons and in each canton, a particular ethnic group would dominate. Of course, in theory the idea would be that those who did not belong to the dominant ethnic groups would also exist with full minority protection and human rights, but that was a far cry from the reality on the ground, which was that as a minority, your chances of being persecuted were overwhelming as distinct from the chances that you could live in safety and pursue living. In many cases, which ethnic group was dominant was not a demographic question, it was a question of how many people had been cleansed from a particular area, and how many people who may have been displaced from elsewhere had been resettled there. There was a great deal of playing with demography as a means of possibly affecting the outcome of the Vance-Owen negotiations. There was also a sense, because of the tremendous gains which the Bosnian Serbs had made and the fact that the Vance-Owen Plan ratified those gains in many respects by recognising it as a fait accompli, that the other parties may wish to do the same in order to achieve the same result. The sense was perhaps that the Croat leadership, Bosnian Croat leadership in Herzegovina, wanted to ensure that they were numerically dominant in places such as Travnik, in places such as Mostar, that there are no pockets of potential Muslim resistance should the Muslims over time begin to resist domination by the Croats, and to a certain extent the notion that if the ethnic configuration, if there was a demographic shift, that the chances that the Vance-Owen Plan would be changed in favour of the Muslim would be that much less. That was just the general sense of how politics were played out in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in this very case, this playing out was total cleansing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apparently that was the idea, that either the Muslims would submit unconditionally to the domination of the HDZ, to the domination of HVO and so on and so forth in the area, or that there would be certain reprisals. I am not sure what the outcome would have been had there been a different, let us say if the entire Muslim population agreed to disarm and to give Travnik and Zenica to the Croats and had been completely compliant, I have no idea what the outcome would have been, that is purely speculative, but there was a willingness in Bosnia-Herzegovina among certain parties to resort to ethnic cleansing as a means of executing their political designs. That unfortunately was the norm and the exception was to respect multi-ethnic co-existence and human rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, the Tribunal would like to thank you for all the clarifications and details which you have given to us about the mission which you were given and which are of use to the International Tribunal. We will now take a 25 minute break and start again at 4.55. The hearing is adjourned. (4.25 pm) (A short break) (4.55 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Ms. Paterson?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. The people would respectfully request that the court permit us to call the next witness as the first witness tomorrow morning. This witness has been waiting all day to testify, the witness will have to give some very difficult testimony and has requested, if court would be agreeable, that it would be preferable for the witness to give all of the testimony in one sitting, to not break it up with a break over the evening recess. Since we are nearly at the end of the day, if there is no objection to the court, we would like to start with this witness first thing in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Since we are speaking about organisation -- Mr. Dubuisson -- this is a private session, is it? All right, we are in private session. (In closed session)
